topic_tag: an expressway and a mill town
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: In a 1990 study, one planner argued that the expressway had, above all, ______ the town.

worlds.passage: In 1958 an expressway was built up a river valley, joining a mill town of eight thousand people to a growing city twenty miles south. Its one exit lay at the edge of town, where the road set off south through open dairy country. Within a decade the mill's younger workers were making that forty-minute drive to city jobs each morning, and their families made it again on Saturdays to shop, while their houses in town stayed full. By 1990 the main street's forty stores had dwindled to eleven. In a 1990 study, one planner argued that the expressway had, above all, ______ the town.
worlds.explanation: The town's people stayed in their houses while their work and their shopping went forty minutes south, and its main street dwindled from forty stores to eleven, so the expressway "drained" it. "Engulfed" fails because the drive south still ran through open dairy country, so the city had not spread to the town. "Fragmented" fails because the road's one exit lay at the edge of town, so it did not run through the streets. "Fossilized" fails because a main street that lost most of its stores was changed, not kept as it was.

engulfed.why: The city was still a long drive away through farmland, so its spread had not reached the town.
engulfed.surface_fit: A small town joined by a new expressway to a growing city twenty miles away is the textbook case of a town swallowed by the city's suburbs.
engulfed.inference: Workers drove forty minutes through open dairy country to reach the city; a town swallowed by a growing city would have houses and stores running out to it, not farms, so the city drew the town's people toward itself from a distance instead of covering it.

fragmented.quote: Its one exit lay at the edge of town
fragmented.why: The road met the town only at its edge, so it ran through no streets and split nothing.
fragmented.surface_fit: Expressways built in the 1950s are famous for cutting towns apart, and a planner saying a highway "fragmented the town" is an ordinary sentence about exactly this kind of project.
fragmented.inference: The expressway touched the town at a single exit on its edge and headed off through farmland, so no neighborhood lay on its far side; a road that only grazes a town's edge cannot cut the town into pieces.

fossilized.why: Losing most of the main street's stores is a large change, not preservation.
fossilized.surface_fit: A mill town whose main street was never rebuilt after 1958 is easy to picture as frozen in that year, and the word suits a planner looking back thirty years later.
fossilized.inference: A fossilized town is one held in its old form; here the workers' jobs moved to the city and twenty-nine of forty stores closed, so the town's daily life was transformed even though its houses stayed full.

worlds.passage: In 1958 an expressway was built up a river valley, joining a mill town of eight thousand people to a growing city twenty miles south. It ran through the town on a raised bank along the old rail line, between the mill and the streets where most of its workers lived, and its nearest exit was in the next town. Within a decade those streets had a grocery, a school and a fire company of their own, a few hundred yards from the ones that still served the mill side. In a 1990 study, one planner argued that the expressway had, above all, ______ the town.
worlds.explanation: The raised road ran between the mill and the workers' streets, and those streets soon had their own grocery, school and fire company a few hundred yards from the old ones, so the expressway split the town in two: it "fragmented" it. "Drained" fails because the road had no exit in town, and the new shops and services opened inside it. "Engulfed" fails because with no exit nearer than the next town, the city's spread had no way in. "Fossilized" fails because a town that built a second grocery, school and fire company changed.

drained.quote: its nearest exit was in the next town
drained.why: With no exit in town the road gave residents no easy way to the city, and new services opened in town instead.
drained.surface_fit: An expressway to a growing city is the usual story of a small town losing its shoppers and workers to that city, and "drained the town" is how planners describe it.
drained.inference: The expressway ran through the town without an exit, so it did not carry the town's workers and shoppers off to the city; what followed was a new grocery, school and fire company inside the town, which is business added, not drawn away.

engulfed.quote: nearest exit was in the next town
engulfed.why: The road could bring no growth into the town, which had no exit of its own.
engulfed.surface_fit: A small town joined by a new expressway to a growing city twenty miles away is the textbook case of a town swallowed by the city's suburbs.
engulfed.inference: A city spreads along an expressway through its exits; this road passed through the town on a bank with no way off it until the next town, so the city's houses and offices had no route in.

fossilized.quote: a grocery, a school and a fire company of their own
fossilized.why: Building new services is change, so the town was not held as it was.
fossilized.surface_fit: A mill town whose main street was never rebuilt after 1958 is easy to picture as frozen in that year, and the word suits a planner looking back thirty years later.
fossilized.inference: The workers' side of the town built its own grocery, school and fire company after the road came, rearranging where half the town shopped, studied and was protected; a fossilized town keeps its old arrangement untouched.

worlds.passage: In 1958 an expressway was built up a river valley, joining a mill town of eight thousand people to a growing city twenty miles south. Its exit at the town's northern edge drew builders, and within a decade the dairy farms between the town and the city had been sold for houses. By 1990 a driver from the city passed no open field before the town's exit, its mill held a city insurer's offices, and its main street was lined with branches of the city's chains. In a 1990 study, one planner argued that the expressway had, above all, ______ the town.
worlds.explanation: The farms between the town and the city were built over until a driver from the city passed no field before reaching it, and city firms filled its mill and main street, so the city's growth rolled over the town: the expressway "engulfed" it. "Drained" fails because the city's firms and houses moved into the town rather than its life moving out. "Fragmented" fails because the exit lay at the northern edge, so the road did not run through the town. "Fossilized" fails because a mill turned into offices and a main street of chains is a transformed town.

drained.quote: lined with branches of the city's chains
drained.why: The main street filled with the city's stores, so business came into the town rather than leaving it.
drained.surface_fit: An expressway to a growing city is the usual story of a small town losing its shoppers and workers to that city, and "drained the town" is how planners describe it.
drained.inference: Chain stores and an insurer from the city look like the town's life passing to outsiders, but the main street was lined with stores and the mill was full of offices; activity was arriving in the town from the city, not flowing out of it.

fragmented.quote: Its exit at the town's northern edge
fragmented.why: The road met the town at its edge, so it cut through no streets.
fragmented.surface_fit: Expressways built in the 1950s are famous for cutting towns apart, and a planner saying a highway "fragmented the town" is an ordinary sentence about exactly this kind of project.
fragmented.inference: The expressway's exit lay at the town's northern edge, and the building spread from there across the farms toward the city; a road at the edge of a town leaves no part of the town on its far side, so the town grew around it without being split.

fossilized.quote: its mill held a city insurer's offices
fossilized.why: The mill no longer made anything, so the town's old form had been replaced.
fossilized.surface_fit: A mill town whose main street was never rebuilt after 1958 is easy to picture as frozen in that year, and the word suits a planner looking back thirty years later.
fossilized.inference: A fossilized town keeps its old life; this town's mill had become offices for a city insurer and its stores had become city chains, so the very things that made it a mill town were replaced.

worlds.passage: In 1958 an expressway was built up a river valley, joining a mill town of eight thousand people to a growing city twenty miles south. Its nearest exit lay nine miles away across the river, and the trucks that had crawled down the main street took the new road. The mill shipped by rail and kept its orders. In 1990 the planner found the families of 1958 behind most of the main street's counters, and its newest building was the 1951 post office. In a 1990 study, one planner argued that the expressway had, above all, ______ the town.
worlds.explanation: With traffic gone and nothing else changed (the mill's orders kept, the same families at the counters, no building newer than 1951), the expressway left the town held in its 1958 form: it "fossilized" it. "Drained" fails because the mill kept its orders and the families kept their stores; only through traffic left. "Engulfed" and "fragmented" both fail because the road ran across the river with its nearest exit nine miles off, so the city's spread could not reach the town and the road cut through none of it.

drained.quote: the families of 1958 behind most of the main street's counters
drained.why: The same families still ran the stores and the mill kept its orders, so nothing of the town's own left.
drained.surface_fit: An expressway to a growing city is the usual story of a small town losing its shoppers and workers to that city, and "drained the town" is how planners describe it.
drained.inference: Losing the traffic down its main street looks like a town being bled, but the mill kept its orders and the 1958 families still kept most of the stores thirty years on; what left was through traffic that had only been passing, so the town's own work and trade stayed.

engulfed.quote: nine miles away across the river
engulfed.why: With the road across the river and no exit near, the city's spread could not reach the town.
engulfed.surface_fit: A small town joined by a new expressway to a growing city twenty miles away is the textbook case of a town swallowed by the city's suburbs.
engulfed.inference: A city spreads along an expressway through its exits; the nearest one was nine miles off on the far side of the river, so new houses following the road could not reach the town, and in 1990 its newest building still dated from 1951.

fragmented.quote: nearest exit lay nine miles away across the river
fragmented.why: The road ran on the far side of the river, so it cut through nothing in the town.
fragmented.surface_fit: Expressways built in the 1950s are famous for cutting towns apart, and a planner saying a highway "fragmented the town" is an ordinary sentence about exactly this kind of project.
fragmented.inference: An expressway splits a town by running through it; this one ran across the river, with the river between it and every street, so no part of the town was cut off from another.

topic_tag: radio and a country's newspapers
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Writing in 1960, one press historian concluded that radio had ______ the country's newspapers.

worlds.passage: In 1925 each large city in one country had its own daily newspaper, and the papers jointly owned the wire service that supplied their national news. The wire service soon sold its bulletins to the new radio stations as well, and by 1940 the stations read each day's main stories aloud at noon; the papers, printed at dawn, carried those stories a day after listeners had heard them. Circulation and advertising kept rising as each paper filled the space national stories had held with its own city's courts, schools and sports. Writing in 1960, one press historian concluded that radio had ______ the country's newspapers.
worlds.explanation: Listeners heard each day's main stories at noon, a day before the papers could print them, so radio took the papers' place as the first source of news without weakening them: it "dethroned" them. "Hamstrung" fails because circulation and advertising kept rising. "Homogenized" fails because each paper filled its pages with its own city's news, which made the papers less alike. "Fractured" fails because the papers sold their bulletins to radio together, through the service they jointly owned.

hamstrung.why: Rising sales and advertising mean the papers had more means to do their work, not less.
hamstrung.surface_fit: The arrival of radio is often said to have crippled newspapers by taking their advertising, so "hamstrung" is a natural verdict on what radio did to the press.
hamstrung.inference: Advertising and circulation pay for a paper's reporters and pages, and both rose; radio took the first telling of the news from the papers but left them better funded, so their ability to work was not crippled.

homogenized.quote: with its own city's courts, schools and sports
homogenized.why: Each paper turned to its own city's news, which differs from city to city.
homogenized.surface_fit: Radio built a single national audience, and historians often say mass media of that era made regional papers all alike, so "homogenized" reads naturally here.
homogenized.inference: The papers all took their national news from one service, but that was true before radio; what radio changed was that each paper moved its space to its own city's courts, schools and sports, which are different everywhere, so radio made the papers less alike.

fractured.quote: The wire service soon sold its bulletins
fractured.why: The papers' jointly owned service made the deal with radio as one body.
fractured.surface_fit: Deals with radio stations really did split press associations in this period, and with the papers sharing one wire service, "fractured" is an obvious thing radio could have done to them.
fractured.inference: The bulletins went to radio through the wire service the papers owned together, so the papers dealt with the stations as a single body; a deal they made jointly is not what split them.

worlds.passage: In 1925 each large city in one country had its own daily newspaper, and the papers jointly owned the wire service that supplied their national news. Radio stations had no reporters and read the papers' stories aloud only after the papers were out. Advertisers moved their money to the stations, and by 1940 most papers had cut two thirds of their pages and every bureau outside their own city, filling the rest with that city's courts and council. They had voted together to cut the wire service to the one daily bulletin they could afford. Writing in 1960, one press historian concluded that radio had ______ the country's newspapers.
worlds.explanation: Losing their advertisers cost the papers two thirds of their pages, every outside bureau and most of their wire service, so they could no longer cover what they once had: radio "hamstrung" them. "Dethroned" fails because radio read the papers' stories only after the papers were out, so print still told the news first. "Homogenized" fails because the pages left went to each city's own courts and council. "Fractured" fails because the papers voted together on cutting the wire service.

dethroned.quote: only after the papers were out
dethroned.why: Radio repeated what the papers had already printed, so print still told the news first.
dethroned.surface_fit: Radio is famous for having taken over from print as the first place people heard the news, so "dethroned the country's newspapers" is a stock judgment for a press historian to make.
dethroned.inference: With no reporters of its own, radio could broadcast a story only after a paper had printed it, so anyone who wanted the news first still had to read it; radio took the papers' money, not their place as the first source.

homogenized.quote: filling the rest with that city's courts and council
homogenized.why: The pages that survived went to local news, which differs in every city.
homogenized.surface_fit: Radio built a single national audience, and historians often say mass media of that era made regional papers all alike, so "homogenized" reads naturally here.
homogenized.inference: Closing outside bureaus and shrinking sounds like papers falling back on the same copy, but the space left went to each city's own courts and council, and even the shared wire was cut back; the papers ended up more local, not more alike.

fractured.quote: voted together to cut the wire service
fractured.why: The papers made their cuts as one body, so radio did not split them.
fractured.surface_fit: Deals with radio stations really did split press associations in this period, and with the papers sharing one wire service, "fractured" is an obvious thing radio could have done to them.
fractured.inference: Cutting the shared wire service was a joint vote the papers took and carried out together; papers that answer hard times by deciding together have been weakened, not broken into camps.

worlds.passage: In 1925 each large city in one country had its own daily newspaper, and the papers jointly owned the wire service that supplied their national news. Radio stations broadcast music and comedy and left the news to the papers. Their programs made the same few comedians and commentators famous in every city, and the papers' owners quarreled for a year over whether to buy those stars' columns through the wire service in place of local writers' work; in the end every paper did, and found that the columns sold better. Writing in 1960, one press historian concluded that radio had ______ the country's newspapers.
worlds.explanation: Radio made the same stars famous everywhere, and in the end every paper bought those stars' columns through the shared wire service in place of local writers' work, so radio made the papers alike: it "homogenized" them. "Dethroned" fails because radio left the news to the papers. "Hamstrung" fails because the columns sold better, so the change was made from strength. "Fractured" fails because the owners' quarrel ended with every paper doing the same thing.

dethroned.quote: left the news to the papers
dethroned.why: Radio did not take over the news, so the papers kept their place.
dethroned.surface_fit: Radio is famous for having taken over from print as the first place people heard the news, so "dethroned the country's newspapers" is a stock judgment for a press historian to make.
dethroned.inference: Radio stations carried entertainment and left news to the papers, so the papers stayed the place people learned the news; radio changed what filled the papers, not their rank.

hamstrung.quote: found that the columns sold better
hamstrung.why: The papers dropped local writers for columns that sold better, a choice made from strength.
hamstrung.surface_fit: The arrival of radio is often said to have crippled newspapers by taking their advertising, so "hamstrung" is a natural verdict on what radio did to the press.
hamstrung.inference: Replacing local writers looks like a paper losing its means, but the papers did it because the stars' columns sold better; they traded one kind of page for a more profitable one, so their capacity to work was not crippled.

fractured.quote: in the end every paper did
fractured.why: The owners' quarrel ended with all the papers making the same choice, so it did not split them.
fractured.surface_fit: Deals with radio stations really did split press associations in this period, and with the papers sharing one wire service, "fractured" is an obvious thing radio could have done to them.
fractured.inference: The year-long quarrel looks like the start of a split, but it ended with every paper buying the same columns through the service they owned together; a dispute that ends in a common purchase has drawn the papers together, not broken them apart.

worlds.passage: In 1925 each large city in one country had its own daily newspaper, and the papers jointly owned the wire service that supplied their national news. Radio stations, which had no reporters, offered to pay for the wire service's bulletins. Papers in the larger cities voted to sell; the rest refused, fearing listeners would stop buying papers. In 1934 the larger papers began taking their national news from a new service the stations helped fund, and spent the stations' money opening bureaus in every province. Writing in 1960, one press historian concluded that radio had ______ the country's newspapers.
worlds.explanation: Radio's offer divided the papers, and the larger ones left the service they had jointly owned for a new one the stations helped fund, so radio "fractured" the country's newspapers. "Dethroned" fails because the stations had no reporters and depended on the papers' bulletins. "Hamstrung" fails because the larger papers used the stations' money to open new bureaus. "Homogenized" fails because the papers now took their national news from two services, where before they had shared one.

dethroned.why: Radio had to buy its news from the papers, so the papers remained its source.
dethroned.surface_fit: Radio is famous for having taken over from print as the first place people heard the news, so "dethroned the country's newspapers" is a stock judgment for a press historian to make.
dethroned.inference: The stations wanted the bulletins because they had no reporters of their own, so whatever radio broadcast came from the papers' services; a medium that depends on the papers for its news has not taken their place.

hamstrung.quote: spent the stations' money opening bureaus
hamstrung.why: The larger papers expanded with radio's money, so they were not crippled.
hamstrung.surface_fit: The arrival of radio is often said to have crippled newspapers by taking their advertising, so "hamstrung" is a natural verdict on what radio did to the press.
hamstrung.inference: Radio's payments let the larger papers open bureaus in every province, more coverage than they had before; papers that grow their reporting because of radio have not had their ability to work cut down.

homogenized.quote: a new service the stations helped fund
homogenized.why: Two services now supplied national news where one had, so the papers grew less alike.
homogenized.surface_fit: Radio built a single national audience, and historians often say mass media of that era made regional papers all alike, so "homogenized" reads naturally here.
homogenized.inference: Before 1934 every paper took its national news from the one shared wire service; afterward the larger papers took it from a different service with its own bureaus, so two versions of the national news ran where there had been one.

topic_tag: an island in a strait
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: One historian has argued that through the nineteenth century the island served those cities above all as their ______.

worlds.passage: A rocky island of two square miles, with a stone quay, lies in a strait between the ocean and an inland sea lined with port cities. The strait's only deep channel runs beneath the island's cliffs, among shoals that no outside captain knew. Every inbound ship came alongside the quay for the cities' customs clerks to open its hatches, and left within the hour with an island pilot at the helm for the forty miles to the cities. One historian has argued that through the nineteenth century the island served those cities above all as their ______.
worlds.explanation: Every ship bound for the cities had to come in under the island's cliffs, was cleared by the cities' customs clerks at its quay, and was taken through the shoals by an island pilot, so the island was the way in to the cities: their "gateway." "Depot" and "haven" fail because each ship left within the hour, so nothing was stored and no ship stayed. "Fortress" fails because the cities posted customs clerks there, who could inspect ships but not stop an enemy.

depot.why: Ships stayed only long enough to be inspected, so nothing was unloaded or stocked.
depot.surface_fit: The island has a quay and a row of warehouses on the sea route to the cities, which is just what a depot is, so a historian calling it the cities' depot reads naturally at first sight.
depot.inference: Every ship stopped at the quay, which is what makes the island look like a supply station, but each left within the hour with its hatches closed again; a depot holds stocks for later, and nothing was put ashore to be kept.

haven.quote: left within the hour with an island pilot
haven.why: Ships stopped only for clearance and went straight on, so none stayed for shelter.
haven.surface_fit: A lone island with a quay at the mouth of an inland sea is exactly where ships would shelter from bad weather, and "served those cities as their haven" is a natural phrase for a historian of shipping.
haven.inference: A haven is somewhere ships wait until it is safe; these ships stopped for an hour to be cleared and then sailed on with a pilot, so the stop was a formality on the way in, not a refuge.

fortress.why: The cities' men on the island were clerks checking cargo, who could not hold off an attack.
fortress.surface_fit: An island planted in the strait that leads to the cities is the textbook site for defending them, so "fortress" is the first role many readers would give it.
fortress.inference: Every ship had to pass close under the island's cliffs, just where guns would command the channel, yet the men the cities posted there opened hatches; an island staffed to inspect cargo could control trade but could not keep an enemy out.

worlds.passage: A rocky island of two square miles, with a stone quay, lies in a strait between the ocean and an inland sea lined with port cities. A hook of rock closes a deep bay on its landward side, and a lighthouse on the hook shows the way in. When winter gales blew down the strait, ships bound for the cities ran into the bay and waited, sometimes for weeks, their crews buying bread from the islanders' ovens; in calm weather they passed the island on either side. One historian has argued that through the nineteenth century the island served those cities above all as their ______.
worlds.explanation: Ships ran into the island's enclosed bay only when gales blew down the strait and waited there until it was safe to go on, so the island served the cities' shipping as a "haven." "Depot" fails because the crews bought bread the islanders baked for them, not stocks kept for the cities. "Gateway" fails because in calm weather ships passed the island on either side. "Fortress" fails because the work on the bay's mouth is a lighthouse that brings every ship in.

depot.quote: buying bread from the islanders' ovens
depot.why: Crews bought what the islanders baked while they waited, not stocks kept to supply the cities.
depot.surface_fit: The island has a quay and a row of warehouses on the sea route to the cities, which is just what a depot is, so a historian calling it the cities' depot reads naturally at first sight.
depot.inference: Ships taking on food at an island quay looks like a supply station, but the crews were buying fresh bread from the islanders because they were stuck there; nothing was shipped in and stored to supply the cities' vessels.

gateway.quote: passed the island on either side
gateway.why: In ordinary weather traffic went past the island without touching it.
gateway.surface_fit: The island sits in the only strait between the ocean and the cities' sea, so calling it their gateway is a phrase a reader expects before reading further.
gateway.inference: In calm weather ships sailed by on both sides, so the way into the inland sea did not run through the island; ships came only when the weather drove them, which makes it a shelter beside the entrance, not the entrance itself.

fortress.quote: a lighthouse on the hook shows the way in
fortress.why: The one work on the bay's mouth guides ships in; nothing was built to keep any out.
fortress.surface_fit: An island planted in the strait that leads to the cities is the textbook site for defending them, so "fortress" is the first role many readers would give it.
fortress.inference: The structure guarding the bay's mouth is a lighthouse that leads ships in at night, so the bay was made easy to enter for any ship; a fortress makes an approach hard for an enemy, and this one was lit to help every ship in.

worlds.passage: A rocky island of two square miles, with a stone quay, lies in a strait between the ocean and an inland sea lined with port cities. Each summer, colliers from a mine across the ocean heaped coal behind the quay. All year the cities' steamships, which burned a ton of coal an hour, put in there on every voyage out and back, while sailing ships, which burned nothing, sailed straight through the strait. The coal was handled by two hundred dockworkers who lived in boardinghouses beside it. One historian has argued that through the nineteenth century the island served those cities above all as their ______.
worlds.explanation: Coal brought in each summer was kept behind the quay and drawn on all year by the cities' steamships on every voyage, so the island was their "depot." "Haven" fails because the steamships called on every voyage because their fuel was there, not to escape storms. "Gateway" fails because sailing ships went straight through without stopping. "Fortress" fails because the island's people were dockworkers handling coal.

haven.quote: on every voyage out and back
haven.why: The steamships called on a fixed round for fuel, in any weather, not to escape storms.
haven.surface_fit: A lone island with a quay at the mouth of an inland sea is exactly where ships would shelter from bad weather, and "served those cities as their haven" is a natural phrase for a historian of shipping.
haven.inference: Ships that stop on every single voyage, both ways, are keeping a refueling schedule set by how much coal they burn; a stop made every time whatever the weather is made for what is stored there, not to shelter from a storm.

gateway.quote: sailing ships, which burned nothing, sailed straight through
gateway.why: Ships that needed no coal ignored the island, so the way into the sea did not run through it.
gateway.surface_fit: The island sits in the only strait between the ocean and the cities' sea, so calling it their gateway is a phrase a reader expects before reading further.
gateway.inference: Sailing ships, needing no coal, passed through the strait without stopping, so traffic into the inland sea did not depend on the island; the steamships stopped only because the coal was kept there.

fortress.quote: two hundred dockworkers who lived in boardinghouses
fortress.why: The island's people were coal handlers, with nothing to defend it.
fortress.surface_fit: An island planted in the strait that leads to the cities is the textbook site for defending them, so "fortress" is the first role many readers would give it.
fortress.inference: The people on the island were dockworkers lodged beside the coal heaps to load the steamships; an island manned to shovel coal supplied the cities' fleet but had no garrison to keep an enemy away from the strait.

worlds.passage: A rocky island of two square miles, with a stone quay, lies in a strait between the ocean and an inland sea lined with port cities. In 1810 the cities placed guns on its heights that reached across the whole strait, and merchant ships sailed past beneath them without stopping. In three wars enemy fleets reached the strait, lost ships to the island's guns, and turned back without entering the inland sea, and each time the island withstood a siege of months. One historian has argued that through the nineteenth century the island served those cities above all as their ______.
worlds.explanation: Enemy fleets that reached the strait were driven back by the island's guns, and the island outlasted every siege, so it held the cities' enemies off: it was their "fortress." "Gateway" and "depot" fail because merchant ships sailed past without stopping, so the island neither handled the cities' traffic nor stocked anything for it. "Haven" fails because a place repeatedly besieged for months could shelter no ship.

gateway.quote: merchant ships sailed past beneath them without stopping
gateway.why: Trade went by the island without any dealings with it, so it was not the way in for the cities' traffic.
gateway.surface_fit: The island sits in the only strait between the ocean and the cities' sea, so calling it their gateway is a phrase a reader expects before reading further.
gateway.inference: Merchant ships bound for the cities sailed on past without touching the island, so the cities' trade did not pass through it; what the island did was stop enemies with its guns, which makes it a stronghold beside the passage, not the passage itself.

depot.quote: sailed past beneath them without stopping
depot.why: Ships did not stop at the island, so nothing was loaded or stocked there for them.
depot.surface_fit: The island has a quay and a row of warehouses on the sea route to the cities, which is just what a depot is, so a historian calling it the cities' depot reads naturally at first sight.

blank_sentence: In a 1905 study, one folklorist argued that centuries of village retelling had, above all, ______ the tale.

worlds.passage: In 1650 a printed collection brought to a mountain region a long tale, set in a distant desert capital, of a merchant's son who outwits a robber king. The printed tale ran to forty pages and eleven episodes. The village versions recorded around 1900 took about three minutes to tell: what remained was the robber king's riddle of the desert's three wells and the son's answer, and a collector who read the 1650 riddle aloud found that villagers could finish each line of it for him. In a 1905 study, one folklorist argued that centuries of village retelling had, above all, ______ the tale.
worlds.explanation: Forty pages and eleven episodes had been reduced to a three-minute telling of the riddle and its answer, so village retelling had "distilled" the tale. "Honed" fails because villagers could finish each line of the 1650 riddle, so its wording had not been reworked. "Domesticated" fails because the riddle was still about the desert's three wells. "Fused" fails because what remained was one piece of the original, with nothing joined to it.

honed.quote: could finish each line of it for him
honed.why: Villagers still knew the printed wording line by line, so tellers had cut the tale without reworking it.
honed.surface_fit: Folklorists often describe oral retelling as sharpening a story with each telling, so "honed the tale" fits both the sentence and the subject.
honed.inference: Honing a story means reworking its wording until it lands harder; villagers could complete the 1650 riddle line by line when a collector read it, so the words that survived were the printed ones, and the tellers' change was to drop the rest.

domesticated.why: The surviving episode still turned on the desert, so the tale had not been moved into the villagers' world.
domesticated.surface_fit: A tale set in a faraway desert and retold for centuries by mountain villagers invites the idea that they made it their own, which is what "domesticated" says.
domesticated.inference: A domesticated tale is moved into its tellers' own landscape; the one episode left was a riddle about the desert's three wells, so even the core the villagers kept stayed in the far-off desert.

fused.quote: what remained was the robber king's riddle
fused.why: Only one piece of the original survived, so no other story had been joined to it.
fused.surface_fit: Oral tales are known to merge with other local stories over time, so a folklorist saying retelling "fused the tale" with local material reads naturally.
fused.inference: Fusing joins a tale to other material, which makes it larger; the village versions held only the riddle and its answer in three minutes, so retelling took the story down to one piece rather than combining it with anything.

"Domesticated" fails because the riddle rhymed on the names of the desert's wells, so the tale was still set in the desert.

distilled.inference: Distilling a tale reduces it to its essentials, which would shorten it; a telling as long as reading the forty printed pages has kept its material, so the tellers changed how it was told without cutting it.

topic_tag: an oasis on a caravan road
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: In a history of the road, one scholar described the oasis as, above all, the desert's ______.

worlds.passage: For six centuries an oasis of palms and wells stood alone on the caravan road across a desert, eleven days from the river and nine from the coast. Caravans from the river and from the coast both unloaded there, and merchants of a dozen peoples kept shops around its wells, buying each load and selling it on to a caravan bound the other way, so that few loads ever crossed the whole desert. Their surviving ledgers record sales in every week of the year. In a history of the road, one scholar described the oasis as, above all, the desert's ______.
worlds.explanation: Merchants of a dozen peoples bought each caravan's load and sold it to one going the other way, in every week of the year, so the oasis was the desert's great market: its "emporium." "Fairground" fails because the ledgers show trade every week, not at one season. "Gatehouse" fails because few loads crossed the desert; caravans sold at the oasis and turned back. "Estate" fails because merchants of a dozen peoples kept their own shops there.

fairground.why: Trade went on every week, so the oasis was not a seasonal gathering place.
fairground.surface_fit: Desert oases are well known as places where scattered herders and traders gathered, so calling one the desert's fairground fits both the sentence and the subject.
fairground.inference: A fairground comes alive for a set season and stands empty between; the merchants' ledgers show sales in every week of the year, so the trade was continuous rather than gathered into a fair.

gatehouse.quote: few loads ever crossed the whole desert
gatehouse.why: Caravans ended their journeys at the oasis, so it controlled no passage across the desert.

worlds.passage: For six centuries an oasis of palms and wells stood alone on the caravan road across a desert, eleven days from the river and nine from the coast. For eleven months its wells served only a few families who grew their own dates. Each spring, when the rains brought grass, herders from every part of the desert and caravans from both ends of the road met there for a month of camel races, weddings, swapped animals and settled feuds, and then scattered back the way they had come. fairground.inference: The autumn harvest did bring a season of activity, but it was tenant families picking dates for the family's camels; a fairground draws many peoples to trade and celebrate, and this was one owner's labor force at work.

gatehouse.inference: A gatehouse earns its name by controlling and taxing passage; caravans watered at this oasis without paying, so the family let traffic pass freely and made its money from its own dates.

topic_tag: stoats and a farmland hedge
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: After six years of tracking collared stoats there, one ecologist concluded that the animals used the hedge above all as their ______.

worlds.passage: A single hawthorn hedge runs a mile east to west across open plowed fields between two oak woods, and voles burrow thickly in the bank beneath it. Young stoats dispersing each autumn from farms south of the valley toward the hills to its north reached the hedge before dawn, slept through the day in old burrows in its bank, and went on north across the fields at nightfall; by winter their collars placed them in the hills, a week's travel away. After six years of tracking collared stoats there, one ecologist concluded that the animals used the hedge above all as their ______.
worlds.explanation: Young stoats on their way north stopped in the hedge for a single day's sleep and went on, so it was their "inn." "Lane" fails because they were traveling south to north while the hedge runs east to west, so it lay across their route rather than along it. "Lair" fails because by winter they had settled in the hills a week away. "Larder" fails because their one day in the bank was spent asleep between two nights of travel.

lane.why: The stoats' route ran across the hedge, not along it.
lane.surface_fit: The hedge is the only cover joining two woods across open fields, and an ecologist calling a hedge the animals' lane is an ordinary way to describe a wildlife route. These stoats are travelers.
lane.inference: The hedge runs east to west between the woods, while these stoats were heading from farms in the south to hills in the north, so their route crossed the hedge; they went into it to sleep and out the far side.

lair.quote: by winter their collars placed them in the hills
lair.why: The stoats settled a week's travel away.
lair.surface_fit: Stoats den in hedge banks, and this bank is riddled with burrows they could take over. These stoats slept in them.
lair.inference: Stoats whose collars show them settled in the hills by winter made their homes there; the hedge held them for a day on the way.

larder.why: The stoats' time in the hedge was spent asleep.
larder.surface_fit: The bank is thick with voles, the stoat's main prey, so a hedge full of prey reads naturally as a predator's larder.
larder.inference: They arrived before dawn and left at nightfall, spending the daylight between two nights of travel asleep, and they never returned; a larder is a supply an animal comes back to draw on.

Each night a female's collar showed her heading straight across the fields to the nearer wood and back to the same burrow by dawn. worlds.explanation: Females settled in the bank from spring to late summer and raised young there, going out each night and returning to the same burrow, so the hedge was their "lair." "Larder" fails because each night they went out to the woods and came back, so the bank was their base, not where they fed.

inn.inference: Females that arrived in early spring were still there in late summer, and young born in that time left from it, so the bank was where they settled to raise a family, far longer than a traveler's stop.
