topic_tag: a college farm station in a wheat district
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: In a history of farming on the plains, one economist describes the station as, above all, the district's ______.

worlds.passage: In 1921 a state agricultural college opened a station on forty acres in a wheat-growing district of the plains, two years after drought had closed the district's last seed merchant. Each spring for forty years its staff sowed strains sent by breeders in other states in narrow strips beside the district's usual wheat. After five seasons the station printed each strain's harvests in the county paper, and the district's farmers took up the few strains that had held up. In a history of farming on the plains, one economist describes the station as, above all, the district's ______.
worlds.explanation: Outside strains were grown beside the usual wheat for five seasons and farmers adopted only the ones that held up, so the station was where new wheat was tried first: a "testbed." "Wellspring" fails because the strains were bred in other states; the station sorted them but originated nothing. "Yardstick" fails because the fixed standard in the strips was the district's usual wheat, while the station's own plantings changed with every batch. "Stopgap" fails because the trials ran every spring for forty years, a standing program rather than cover for the closed merchant until trade returned.

wellspring.quote: strains sent by breeders in other states
wellspring.why: The strains came from breeders elsewhere, so the station was not the source of the district's wheat.
wellspring.surface_fit: The new wheats the district took up all came to it through the station, so the station reads at first as the source of the district's wheat.
wellspring.inference: A source has to originate what flows from it; every strain the station handled had been bred in another state, so what it gave the district was a choice among others' wheats, not wheat of its own.

yardstick.why: Each strain was judged against the usual wheat in the next strip, so the usual wheat was the standard, not the station.
yardstick.surface_fit: The station printed harvest figures in the county paper every year, so it can look like the measure the district judged its wheat by.
yardstick.inference: A yardstick stays fixed while other things are measured against it; the station's plots held a new set of outside strains each spring, and the constant they were compared with was the farmers' own usual wheat in the neighboring strip.

stopgap.why: A program running forty years was not a temporary fill-in.
stopgap.surface_fit: The station opened just after drought closed the district's last seed merchant, so a student expects it to have filled that gap until trade returned.
stopgap.inference: A stopgap covers a need only until the normal arrangement returns; trials repeated every spring for forty years, on strains the merchant never sold, were the station's permanent work, not a stand-in for the merchant.

worlds.passage: In 1921 a state agricultural college opened a station on forty acres in a wheat-growing district of the plains, two years after drought had closed the district's last seed merchant. It sowed one strain of the usual wheat on the same plots, by the same methods, every year, and sold each harvest to a flour mill, while farmers ordered their seed by mail. Each autumn the county agent printed the station's yield per acre, and a farmer who had tried a new strain or plow judged it against that figure. In a history of farming on the plains, one economist describes the station as, above all, the district's ______.
worlds.explanation: The station grew the same wheat the same way every year, and farmers judged their own changes against its yield, so it was the district's "yardstick." "Testbed" fails because the trying happened on the farms, where farmers tested new strains and plows; the station changed nothing. "Wellspring" fails because its harvest went to a flour mill, so none of its grain spread to the farms. "Stopgap" fails because farmers were already getting seed by mail, so the station was not filling the closed merchant's place.

testbed.quote: a farmer who had tried a new strain or plow
testbed.why: The new strains and plows were tried on the farms, so the farms, not the station, were where things were tested.
testbed.surface_fit: A college's agricultural station with its own plots is exactly the kind of place a reader expects to be a proving ground.
testbed.inference: A testbed is where new things are tried out; here the farmers did the trying on their own land and needed the station's unchanging plots only as the fixed figure to compare against, so the station was the constant, not the experiment.

wellspring.quote: sold each harvest to a flour mill
wellspring.why: All the station's grain was milled, so nothing from it spread to the farms.
wellspring.surface_fit: Histories of plains farming often credit a college station as the source of a district's agriculture, so the word fits the topic on a first read.
wellspring.inference: A source is something farms draw from; grain that goes to a mill becomes flour and never reaches a field, so the district's wheat could not have flowed from the station.

stopgap.quote: farmers ordered their seed by mail
stopgap.why: Farmers had another seed supply, so the station did not stand in for the closed merchant.
stopgap.surface_fit: The station opened two years after the district lost its last seed merchant and grew the district's own wheat, so it looks like a temporary replacement for him.
stopgap.inference: Standing in for the merchant would mean supplying the seed he had sold; farmers were ordering seed by mail while the station's wheat went to a mill, so the merchant's place was filled by mail-order houses, not by the station.

worlds.passage: In 1921 a state agricultural college opened a station on forty acres in a wheat-growing district of the plains, two years after drought had closed the district's last seed merchant. That spring the station began buying seed wheat by the carload from a merchant three states away and selling it to the district's farmers at cost from its barn. A seed company opened a store in the county seat in 1925, and the next spring the college turned the station's empty barn and idle fields over to cattle. In a history of farming on the plains, one economist describes the station as, above all, the district's ______.
worlds.explanation: The station supplied seed from the year after the merchant closed until a seed store opened, then gave the work up, so it was a temporary fill-in: a "stopgap." "Wellspring" fails because the seed it sold was bought from a merchant three states away; the station passed it on rather than producing it. "Testbed" fails because the station's fields lay idle, so nothing was tried on them. "Yardstick" fails for the same reason: idle fields yielded no figure for farms to be measured against.

wellspring.quote: buying seed wheat by the carload from a merchant three states away
wellspring.why: The seed came from a distant merchant, so the station passed seed on rather than being its source.
wellspring.surface_fit: Seed for every farm in the district went out from the station's barn, which reads like the district's wheat flowing from it.
wellspring.inference: A wellspring is where something originates; seed bought by the carload three states away and resold at cost only passed through the station's barn, so the station was a conduit for another merchant's seed, not its source.

testbed.why: The station's fields were idle, so there was nothing growing on them to be tested.
testbed.surface_fit: An agricultural college opening a farm station in a struggling district suggests a site for trying new crops and methods.
testbed.inference: Trials need plots on which something new is grown; a station whose fields lay idle while it resold another merchant's seed grew nothing, so it could not have been trying anything.

yardstick.why: With nothing grown, the station had no yields for farms to be measured against.
yardstick.surface_fit: The station dealt in the same wheat every farmer grew, so its wheat might look like the standard the district measured its farms against.
yardstick.inference: A yardstick needs a figure of its own to compare with; a station that sold bought-in seed and grew nothing on its fields produced no yield at all, so there was nothing to measure the farms against.

worlds.passage: In 1921 a state agricultural college opened a station on forty acres in a wheat-growing district of the plains, two years after drought had closed the district's last seed merchant. In its first summer its staff found, in a drought-killed field, a few heads of wheat still standing, and from them they raised a strain they named for the district. Each autumn for thirty years they handed a sack of it to any farmer who asked, and by 1950 seed passed between neighbors had carried it into three adjoining counties. In a history of farming on the plains, one economist describes the station as, above all, the district's ______.
worlds.explanation: The district's own hardy strain was raised at the station from a few surviving heads and flowed out from it for thirty years, spreading farm to farm into three counties, so the station was the district's "wellspring." "Testbed" fails because the station raised and handed out one strain year after year; it tried nothing against anything. "Stopgap" fails because it handed out its own new strain for thirty years, not the merchant's seed until a store reopened. "Yardstick" fails because its harvest went out in sacks as seed, not as a figure farms were compared with.

testbed.quote: Each autumn for thirty years they handed a sack of it
testbed.why: The station multiplied and handed out one strain for decades, which is supplying, not testing.
testbed.surface_fit: A college station raising a new strain from a few surviving heads sounds like experimental plant work, so a student may read it as a proving ground.
testbed.inference: A testbed tries out several things before others adopt the ones that work; this station grew one strain and handed it out every autumn for thirty years, so nothing was being compared or tried on its land.

stopgap.quote: a strain they named for the district
stopgap.why: The station gave out a new strain of its own, not the closed merchant's stock until he returned.
stopgap.surface_fit: The station started handing out seed in the first years after drought closed the last seed merchant, so it looks like a temporary fill-in.
stopgap.inference: A stopgap supplies the usual thing until the normal supplier returns; this station supplied a strain no merchant had ever sold, raised from its own find, and went on doing so for thirty years, so it was not filling a gap until anything returned.

yardstick.quote: handed a sack of it to any farmer who asked
yardstick.why: The station's harvest went out as seed, so it served as a supply, not a standard.
yardstick.surface_fit: Nearly every farm grew the station's strain, so the station could look like the standard the district's farms were measured against.
yardstick.inference: A yardstick is a fixed figure others are judged by; the station's harvest went out each autumn in sacks to be sown, so what the farms took from it was the seed itself, and the comparison a yardstick offers never comes into it.

topic_tag: a dawn auction rule at a fishing port
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Writing in 1960, one economist argued that the rule had ______ the city's fish market.

worlds.passage: In 1931 a port city required every fishing boat landing there to sell its whole catch at a single dawn auction on the quay; before, each crew had sold to any buyer it chose, whenever it chose. Crews could no longer hold fish back for a better price, so every catch reached the quay the morning after it was caught. Inland fish shops, which had sent buyers only after a big catch, placed standing orders for a fixed number of crates at each dawn's auction, and the quay was bare by six. Writing in 1960, one economist argued that the rule had ______ the city's fish market.
worlds.explanation: Every catch now reached the quay on a regular schedule, and inland shops answered with fixed daily orders that cleared it each morning, so supply and demand both became regular and the rule "steadied" the market. "Saturated" fails because the extra fish was all bought by six each morning. "Stifled" fails because more fish was landed and more buyers bought every day than before. "Uprooted" fails because the standing orders were placed at the city's own auction, so the market stayed where it was.

saturated.quote: the quay was bare by six
saturated.why: Everything landed was bought each morning, so there was no glut.
saturated.surface_fit: Crews could no longer hold fish back, so every fish caught now hit the quay at once, which is exactly how a market gets glutted.
saturated.inference: A glut leaves fish unsold; a quay cleared by six every morning, with shops ordering fixed amounts daily, shows the larger landings were matched by buyers.

stifled.quote: placed standing orders for a fixed number of crates
stifled.why: Buyers who had come only now and then ordered every day, so trade grew rather than being choked.
stifled.surface_fit: A rule forcing every crew into one dawn auction sounds like the kind of regulation that chokes a trade, and economists often say such rules stifled a market.
stifled.inference: Choking a trade means less of it happens; shops that once sent buyers only after a big catch now ordered crates at every auction, so more fish changed hands under the rule than before it.

uprooted.why: The orders went to the city's own auction, so the market stayed in place.
uprooted.surface_fit: Moving every sale to one auction on the quay tore up the old way of selling, so a student may read the rule as having pulled the market up from its old footing.
uprooted.inference: Uprooting would move the trade somewhere else; the inland shops tied their orders to the city's dawn auction, so the market's place and its buyers stayed, and only its rhythm changed.

worlds.passage: In 1931 a port city required every fishing boat landing there to sell its whole catch at a single dawn auction on the quay; before, each crew had sold to any buyer it chose, whenever it chose. Crews could no longer hold fish back in their ice holds for a better price, so every fish caught went under the hammer the morning it was landed, while the number of buyers stayed about the same. By 1934 a third of each dawn's catch was going to the fertilizer works at a few cents a crate. Writing in 1960, one economist argued that the rule had ______ the city's fish market.
worlds.explanation: Every fish caught now came to auction at once while the number of buyers stayed the same, until a third of the catch was sold off as fertilizer, so the rule "saturated" the market. "Steadied" fails because fish worth only a few cents a crate means prices had fallen through the floor, not settled. "Stifled" fails because more fish was offered than ever, not less. "Uprooted" fails because every crew still landed and sold at the city's quay.

steadied.quote: at a few cents a crate
steadied.why: A third of the catch selling for pennies as fertilizer shows prices collapsing, not settling.
steadied.surface_fit: One fixed auction at a fixed hour replacing scattered private deals sounds like a way to bring order and steadier prices to a fish market.
steadied.inference: Fish that once sold as food going to fertilizer works at a few cents a crate means the price of a large part of each catch fell to almost nothing, which is the opposite of prices holding at a settled level.

stifled.quote: every fish caught went under the hammer
stifled.why: All of every catch now came to market, so trade was not choked off.
stifled.surface_fit: Losses, unsold fish and a rule forcing everyone into one auction all sound like a regulation that choked the fish trade.
stifled.inference: A stifled market sees less traded; here every fish caught was put up for sale each morning, more than crews had sold before, so the trouble was too much offered, not too little.

uprooted.why: The fish were still landed and sold at the city's quay, so the market did not move.
uprooted.surface_fit: The rule tore up the old way of selling, crew by crew and buyer by buyer, so a student might say it pulled the market up by the roots.
uprooted.inference: Uprooting moves a market away from its place; every catch was still landed at the city's quay and auctioned there each dawn, so the market stayed put and only grew more crowded.

worlds.passage: In 1931 a port city required every fishing boat landing there to sell its whole catch at a single dawn auction on the quay; before, each crew had sold to any buyer it chose, whenever it chose. The crews of small boats, who fished inshore at night, now waited hours for the auction, and within five years half those boats lay idle at their moorings most of the week, their crews working on the docks. With so few boats going out, the price of a crate leapt every time the weather turned. Writing in 1960, one economist argued that the rule had ______ the city's fish market.
worlds.explanation: Half the small boats stopped fishing most of the week while staying at the city's moorings, so the market simply had less to trade: the rule "stifled" it. "Uprooted" fails because those boats sat idle at the city's own moorings rather than fishing and selling somewhere else. "Saturated" fails because fewer boats going out meant less fish, not too much. "Steadied" fails because prices now leapt with every change in the weather.

uprooted.why: The boats stayed in the city, idle, so the trade did not move elsewhere.
uprooted.surface_fit: Half the small boats vanished from the city's auction within five years, which looks like the market being torn from its place.
uprooted.inference: For the market to be uprooted the fishing and selling would have to go on somewhere else; boats lying idle at the city's moorings, their crews on the city's docks, mean the trade did not move, it just stopped.

saturated.quote: With so few boats going out
saturated.why: Fewer boats fishing means less fish, so the market was not flooded.
saturated.surface_fit: A single auction at one hour forcing every catch onto the quay at once is a setting where a reader expects more fish than buyers.
saturated.inference: A glut needs more fish offered than buyers want; half the inshore boats lying idle most of the week cut the supply, so the market had less fish, not too much.

steadied.quote: the price of a crate leapt every time the weather turned
steadied.why: Prices jumped with the weather, so the market was not steadier.
steadied.surface_fit: Replacing private sales at any hour with one regular dawn auction sounds like a measure meant to bring order to a market.
steadied.inference: A steadier market has prices that move less; with so few boats left, any bad weather cut the morning's supply and sent prices leaping, so the swings grew larger.

worlds.passage: In 1931 a port city required every fishing boat landing there to sell its whole catch at a single dawn auction on the quay; before, each crew had sold to any buyer it chose, whenever it chose. A village four miles down the coast, where crews could still sell to any buyer at any hour, built a new quay in 1932. Within two years the city's fish merchants had moved their stalls there, the boats followed them, and carts carried each catch up the coast road to the same city shops as before. Writing in 1960, one economist argued that the rule had ______ the city's fish market.
worlds.explanation: The city's merchants and boats moved to the village quay while the same city shops kept getting their fish by cart, so the rule "uprooted" the market: the whole market went on, in another place. "Stifled" fails because the city's shops were supplied as before, so the city's fish market lost its site, not its trade. "Saturated" fails because the boats landed at the village, so no fish reached the city's quay to glut it. "Steadied" fails because a market whose merchants, boats and quay all moved within two years was overturned, not settled.

stifled.quote: carts carried each catch up the coast road to the same city shops as before
stifled.why: The city's shops still got their fish, so the city's market kept its trade; only its site moved.
stifled.surface_fit: The city's merchants and boats all left the city's quay, so a student reading for decline will take the city's fish market as choked off.
stifled.inference: A stifled market sells less; the same city shops were stocked from the same merchants, who had only moved their stalls four miles, so the city's fish market went on trading at its old volume from a new place.

saturated.why: The boats landed at the village, so no fish arrived at the city's quay to flood it.
saturated.surface_fit: A rule forcing every catch into one dawn auction invites the reading that the city's quay was flooded with more fish than it could sell.
saturated.inference: Saturation needs more fish arriving at the city's auction than its buyers take; the boats followed the merchants to the village quay, so the city's quay received no catch at all.

steadied.why: The merchants moved their whole business within two years, which is an upheaval, not a settling.
steadied.surface_fit: Ordering every sale into one regular auction sounds like a measure that would make a market more orderly and its prices steadier.
steadied.inference: A steadied market keeps its arrangements and evens them out; this one moved its merchants, its boats and its landing place four miles within two years, so its arrangements were overturned.

topic_tag: a volcanic island two decades after an eruption
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Revisiting the island in 1903, one geologist wrote that the eruption had ______ it.

worlds.passage: In 1883 a volcano erupted on a small island off a mountainous coast, where a fishing village had stood above a sheltered harbor for three centuries, with farms on the slopes behind it. Sailing in twenty years later, surveyors moored beside the church tower, whose stone steps, which had once climbed nine meters from the quay to its door, now ran down into the water. The old tide marks cut in the cliffs at both ends of the island lay the same depth under the sea, and the summit farms were planted as before. Revisiting the island in 1903, one geologist wrote that the eruption had ______ it.
worlds.explanation: Steps that once climbed from the quay now run down into the water, and tide marks at both ends lie equally deep under the sea, so the whole island went down: the eruption "submerged" it. "Tilted" fails because the marks at both ends sank by the same amount, so neither end rose. "Scoured" fails because the church tower still stands, so the buildings were not swept away. "Smothered" fails because the summit farms were planted as before, so no deposit buried the island.

tilted.quote: at both ends of the island lay the same depth under the sea
tilted.why: Both ends went down by the same amount, so the island sank level rather than tipping.
tilted.surface_fit: Volcanic islands do heave and tip in eruptions, and a church whose steps now run into the sea is what a tipped island would show at its low end.
tilted.inference: A tilt raises one end and lowers the other, so tide marks at the two ends would move by different amounts; marks at both ends lying equally deep under the sea mean the whole island dropped evenly.

scoured.why: The tower still stands where it stood, so the eruption did not sweep the village away.
scoured.surface_fit: Eruptions send surges and waves that strip coasts bare, and a harbor village no longer reachable on foot suggests it was swept off.
scoured.inference: Scouring carries buildings and soil away; a church tower still standing with its steps in place, now reached by boat, was covered by water, not removed.

smothered.quote: the summit farms were planted as before
smothered.why: Farms still worked means the soil was not buried.
smothered.surface_fit: Burial under what a volcano throws out is the most familiar thing an eruption does to land, so it is a natural first guess for any volcanic island.
smothered.inference: A smothered island has its fields buried and unfarmable for years; summit farms planted as before show their soil was never covered.

worlds.passage: In 1883 a volcano erupted on a small island off a mountainous coast, where a fishing village had stood above a sheltered harbor for three centuries, with farms on the slopes behind it. Sailing in twenty years later, surveyors found the sea caves in the eastern cliffs standing dry, nine meters above the tide, while at the western end spring tides now ran into the doorways of the village's houses, which stood in their old rows. The hill farms between had taken their first harvest the summer after the eruption. Revisiting the island in 1903, one geologist wrote that the eruption had ______ it.
worlds.explanation: The eastern cliffs rose out of the sea while the western village now floods at spring tides, so one end went up and the other down: the eruption "tilted" the island. "Submerged" fails because the eastern end now stands nine meters higher, and the west floods only at the highest tides. "Scoured" fails because the village's houses stand in their old rows. "Smothered" fails because the hill farms were harvested the very next summer.

submerged.quote: standing dry, nine meters above the tide
submerged.why: The eastern end rose, so the island as a whole did not go under.
submerged.surface_fit: Spring tides now run into the village's doorways, which is what an island going down into the sea would show.
submerged.inference: Sea caves cut at the waterline now standing dry nine meters up mean the eastern end rose; an island whose one end climbed out of the sea while the other floods only at spring tides did not go under.

scoured.quote: which stood in their old rows
scoured.why: The houses stand where they stood, so nothing was swept away.
scoured.surface_fit: Eruptions send waves and surges that strip a shore, and houses now taking the tide at their doors suggest a battered, stripped coast.
scoured.inference: Scouring carries houses and soil off; houses still standing in their old rows, with only the tide now reaching them, were left in place while the ground beneath them sank.

smothered.quote: had taken their first harvest the summer after the eruption
smothered.why: The fields were harvested within a year, so nothing had buried them.
smothered.surface_fit: Burial under what a volcano throws out is what most people picture an eruption doing to a farmed island.
smothered.inference: Fields buried by an eruption stay out of use for years; hill farms harvesting the very next summer had soil that was never covered.

worlds.passage: In 1883 a volcano erupted on a small island off a mountainous coast, where a fishing village had stood above a sheltered harbor for three centuries, with farms on the slopes behind it. Landing twenty years later, surveyors dug down through hard gray layers to reach the doorways of the village's houses, and on the slopes only the tops of the orchard walls showed. The tide still reached the old mark cut on the quay steps, and the island's one stream, cutting through the gray, still ran to the harbor along its old bed. Revisiting the island in 1903, one geologist wrote that the eruption had ______ it.
worlds.explanation: Surveyors had to dig down to reach doorways, and only the tops of orchard walls show, so the eruption buried the island where it stood: it "smothered" it. "Scoured" fails because the houses are still there under the layers, so nothing was swept off. "Submerged" fails because the tide still reaches the old mark on the quay steps, so the land did not sink. "Tilted" fails because the stream still runs to the harbor along its old bed, which tipped ground would have turned aside.

scoured.quote: to reach the doorways of the village's houses
scoured.why: The houses are still there beneath the layers, so the surface was covered, not stripped.
scoured.surface_fit: A village that can only be reached by digging sounds like a place wrecked by the eruption's blast, which is what scouring suggests.
scoured.inference: Scouring removes buildings and soil; houses whose doorways can be reached by digging down were left in place and covered over, so the surface was added to, not stripped.

submerged.quote: The tide still reached the old mark cut on the quay steps
submerged.why: The sea reaches the same mark as before, so the land did not sink.
submerged.surface_fit: A harbor village hidden from view after an eruption is the familiar picture of one that has gone down into the sea.
submerged.inference: If the island had sunk, the tide would now rise above the old mark on the quay steps; it still stops at that mark, so the land stands where it stood and the village is hidden by what lies over it.

tilted.quote: still ran to the harbor along its old bed
tilted.why: The stream keeps its old course, so the ground did not tip.
tilted.surface_fit: Ground heaving and tipping is a known effect of eruptions on small islands, and a geologist revisiting one would look for it.
tilted.inference: Water runs downhill, so tipping the island would send its stream off in a new direction; a stream that still follows its old bed to the harbor shows the slopes keep the lean they always had.

worlds.passage: In 1883 a volcano erupted on a small island off a mountainous coast, where a fishing village had stood above a sheltered harbor for three centuries, with farms on the slopes behind it. Landing twenty years later, surveyors found bare rock, scored with grooves running downhill, where the farms and the village had been, and fishermen offshore still snagged roof beams in their nets. The tide still reached the old mark cut in the quay's bedrock, and the island's one stream still ran to the harbor down its old gully. Revisiting the island in 1903, one geologist wrote that the eruption had ______ it.
worlds.explanation: Bare rock grooved downhill where farms and houses stood, with their beams now in the sea, shows that the eruption dragged the surface off: it "scoured" the island. "Smothered" fails because the rock was left bare, with nothing lying over it. "Submerged" fails because the tide still reaches the old mark in the quay's bedrock, so the beams were carried into the sea while the land stayed up. "Tilted" fails because the stream still runs down its old gully, which tipped ground would have turned aside.

smothered.quote: found bare rock, scored with grooves running downhill
smothered.why: Bare, grooved rock means the surface was dragged off, not covered.
smothered.surface_fit: Burial under what a volcano throws out is the most familiar fate of a village beside one, so smothering is the natural first guess.
smothered.inference: Smothering leaves the old surface intact under a deposit; bare rock grooved downhill where soil and houses had been means the old surface was dragged off toward the sea, with nothing left lying over it.

submerged.quote: The tide still reached the old mark cut in the quay's bedrock
submerged.why: The sea reaches the same mark as before, so the land did not go under.
submerged.surface_fit: Roof beams from the village now come up in fishermen's nets offshore, which suggests the village lies under the sea.
submerged.inference: If the island had sunk, the tide would now rise past the old mark in the quay's bedrock; it stops at the same mark, so the land stayed up and the beams were carried out to sea.

tilted.quote: still ran to the harbor down its old gully
tilted.why: The stream keeps its old course, so the ground did not tip.
tilted.surface_fit: Ground heaving and tipping is a known effect of eruptions, and surveyors returning to an island are looking for it.
tilted.inference: Water runs downhill, so a tipped island would send its stream along a new course; a stream still running down its old gully shows the island's slopes are as they were.

topic_tag: a mountain lake above orchards and trout ponds
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: One hydrologist has described the lake as serving the river as a kind of ______.

worlds.passage: A mountain river flows through a narrow lake and then forty miles down to a valley, whose canals feed orchards and trout ponds that fail when the water passes seventy degrees. The lake is three hundred feet deep, and its basin is bare granite, where all snowmelt drains into the river before the river reaches the lake. Its level hardly changes from season to season, and its outlet draws on cold water near the bottom. Above the lake the river freezes in January and runs warm by August; the ponds have never frozen or failed. One hydrologist has described the lake as serving the river as a kind of ______.
worlds.explanation: The river freezes and warms with the seasons above the lake, but the ponds fed from the deep lake's cold bottom water never freeze or overheat, so the lake evens out the river's temperature: a "thermostat." "Tributary" fails because all the basin's snowmelt reaches the river before the lake, so the lake has no water of its own to add. "Sink" fails because bare granite lets no water seep away. "Valve" fails because a lake whose level hardly changes stores nothing to hold back and release.

tributary.quote: drains into the river before the river reaches the lake
tributary.why: All the basin's water is already in the river when it enters the lake, so the lake adds none.
tributary.surface_fit: A big mountain lake above a farming valley is the kind of feature people credit with feeding the valley's river.
tributary.inference: A tributary brings water from some other source; every trickle in this basin joins the river above the lake, so the lake receives only the river's own water and can send down nothing extra.

sink.why: Solid granite lets no water seep away, so the lake cannot swallow the river's water.
sink.surface_fit: A lake three hundred feet deep holds an enormous volume, so it is easy to picture the river's water disappearing into it.
sink.inference: A lake loses a river's water by letting it seep away underground; bare granite holds water rather than leaking it, so whatever comes in must go on out.

valve.quote: Its level hardly changes from season to season
valve.why: A lake whose level stays put holds nothing back, so it cannot be releasing stored water on a schedule.
valve.surface_fit: A deep lake with a single outlet on the only river to the valley looks like the control point for how much water the canals get.
valve.inference: A valve shifts water in time by holding it back and letting it go; holding water back would raise the lake and releasing it would lower it, so a level that hardly changes means the water passes through as it comes.

worlds.passage: A mountain river flows through a narrow lake and then forty miles down to a valley, whose canals feed orchards and trout ponds that fail when the water passes seventy degrees. Springs across the lake's broad, flat floor keep it brimming, and below the outlet the river runs half again as wide as above the lake. In the drought of 1934, when the river above the lake shrank to a trickle, the lake stayed brimming and its outlet kept running, and the ponds, as in every year, were stocked only in spring and fall. One hydrologist has described the lake as serving the river as a kind of ______.
worlds.explanation: Springs keep the lake full and the river leaves it half again as wide, even in a drought, so the lake adds water to the river like a "tributary." "Sink" fails because the river grows in the lake rather than shrinking. "Valve" fails because in the drought the lake stayed brimming while its outlet ran, so the water was not stored water being let out. "Thermostat" fails because the ponds could still be stocked only in spring and fall, so the lake did nothing to keep the water's temperature within their limits.

sink.quote: half again as wide as above the lake
sink.why: The river leaves the lake larger than it entered, so the lake gives water rather than taking it.
sink.surface_fit: Lake beds that swallow river water are familiar, and springs in a lake floor suggest water moving through the ground beneath it.
sink.inference: A sink would leave the river smaller below the lake; a river half again as wide below the outlet carries more water than it brought, so the lake is a net source.

valve.quote: the lake stayed brimming and its outlet kept running
valve.why: The drought outflow did not draw the lake down, so it was not stored water being let go.
valve.surface_fit: A lake that kept the canals running through a drought, when the river above it had shrunk to a trickle, looks like a store being released on purpose, the way a valve lets water through.
valve.inference: Water released from storage lowers a lake; this lake stayed brimming while its outlet ran through the drought, so the water was being supplied as it flowed, from the springs, not held back and let out.

thermostat.quote: were stocked only in spring and fall
thermostat.why: The ponds still could not hold trout in winter or summer, so the lake was not steadying the water's temperature.
thermostat.surface_fit: Lakes are known for moderating the temperature of water passing through them, and the valley's trout ponds depend on just that.
thermostat.inference: The ponds fail when the water freezes or passes seventy degrees; ponds that can be stocked only between the seasons' extremes are getting water that still freezes and still overheats, so the broad, shallow lake moderates nothing.

worlds.passage: A mountain river flows through a narrow lake and then forty miles down to a valley, whose canals feed orchards and trout ponds that fail when the water passes seventy degrees. The lake lies on porous limestone, and water seeps through its floor into caverns that open, miles away, as springs in another valley. Below the outlet the river runs half as wide as above the lake, and in dry summers its bed lies bare; the seepage keeps the lake shallow, so in August the ponds draw on wells. One hydrologist has described the lake as serving the river as a kind of ______.
worlds.explanation: Water seeps through the lake's limestone floor into caverns that empty into another valley, so the river loses half its water there: the lake is a "sink." "Valve" fails because the water missing in dry summers is not held for later; it comes out as springs in another valley. "Tributary" fails because the river leaves the lake half as wide. "Thermostat" fails because the seepage keeps the lake shallow, and the ponds must turn to wells in August.

valve.quote: open, miles away, as springs in another valley
valve.why: The water the lake takes resurfaces in another valley, so it is never let back out to this river.
valve.surface_fit: In dry summers the river bed below the lake lies bare, which looks like a valve shutting off the flow to the canals.
valve.inference: A valve holds water back and later lets it through to the same channel; this lake's missing water surfaces as springs in a different valley, so it never returns to this river at all.

tributary.quote: half as wide as above the lake
tributary.why: The river leaves the lake smaller, so the lake takes water from it.
tributary.surface_fit: A lake high on the river that feeds a farming valley is easily read as one of the river's sources.
tributary.inference: A tributary adds to a river; a river half as wide below the outlet as above the lake, and dry in summer, has lost water in the lake, not gained it.

thermostat.quote: the seepage keeps the lake shallow, so in August the ponds draw on wells
thermostat.why: A shallow lake warms in summer, so its outflow is too warm for the ponds.
thermostat.surface_fit: Lakes are known for moderating temperature, and a hydrologist writing about orchards and trout ponds would look for exactly that.
thermostat.inference: Holding water cool through summer takes depth; a lake drained from below stays shallow, its water warms in the sun, and the ponds must turn to wells in August, so it keeps nothing cool.

worlds.passage: A mountain river flows through a narrow lake and then forty miles down to a valley, whose canals feed orchards and trout ponds that fail when the water passes seventy degrees. Each winter an ice dam forms at the lake's outlet, and the lake rises fifty feet while the channel below runs nearly dry. When the dam breaks in late spring the canals overflow for a few weeks as the lake falls back to its autumn level; by midsummer the drained lake lies shallow in the sun, and the ponds turn to wells. One hydrologist has described the lake as serving the river as a kind of ______.
worlds.explanation: The ice dam shuts the river off each winter and the flow is let through again in spring, so the lake works as a "valve" on the river. "Sink" fails because the water held back all winter reaches the canals in spring. "Tributary" fails because the spring flood only brings the lake back to its autumn level, so it is the river's own winter water returning, not water the lake adds. "Thermostat" fails because the drained lake lies shallow in the sun by midsummer, and the ponds must turn to wells.

sink.quote: the canals overflow for a few weeks
sink.why: The winter's water reaches the canals in spring, so the lake does not keep it.
sink.surface_fit: All winter the river runs into the lake and almost none comes out, which is exactly what a sink for the river would look like.
sink.inference: A sink keeps the water it takes in; the water stored behind the ice floods the canals when the dam breaks, so over the year the river gets it back.

tributary.quote: the lake falls back to its autumn level
tributary.why: The spring flood empties only what winter stored, so the lake adds no water of its own.
tributary.surface_fit: In spring the lake sends far more water down to the canals than the river is bringing in, which reads like the lake feeding the river.
tributary.inference: A tributary supplies water of its own; a flood that ends with the lake back at its autumn level has released exactly what the winter stored, so the lake changed when the water came, not how much.

thermostat.quote: the drained lake lies shallow in the sun
thermostat.why: Once drained the lake is shallow and sun-warmed, so it cannot keep the water cool.
thermostat.surface_fit: A lake fifty feet deeper in winter looks like a large body of water that could keep the river cool for the trout ponds.
thermostat.inference: Keeping summer water cool takes depth; the same release that ends the winter's storage leaves the lake shallow and sunlit by midsummer, so its water warms and the ponds turn to wells.

topic_tag: restoring a sixteenth-century altarpiece
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Reviewing the work in 1960, one curator wrote that the restorers had, above all, ______ the altarpiece.

worlds.passage: In 1952 a museum sent a sixteenth-century altarpiece, painted on three oak panels and darkened by four centuries of candle smoke and varnish, to a restoration workshop for two years. X-rays taken through the oak showed figures beneath the two saints' heavy robes and the clouds above them. Over two years the restorers lifted the robes and clouds, paint added in the 1700s, flake by flake under a microscope, and the altarpiece came home on the same worm-eaten panels, with two kneeling donors in the sky where the clouds had been. Reviewing the work in 1960, one curator wrote that the restorers had, above all, ______ the altarpiece.
worlds.explanation: The X-rays showed figures under the robes and clouds, and lifting that later paint brought kneeling donors back into view, so the restorers "uncovered" the altarpiece. "Scrubbed" fails because the later paint was lifted flake by flake under a microscope, the opposite of harsh cleaning, and only the 1700s layer came off. "Transferred" fails because the altarpiece came home on the same worm-eaten panels. "Stabilized" fails because the work changed what the picture shows instead of securing it as it was.

scrubbed.quote: flake by flake under a microscope
scrubbed.why: Painstaking removal of one later layer is the opposite of harsh overcleaning.
scrubbed.surface_fit: Removing layers from a smoke-darkened altarpiece is the kind of cleaning critics accuse of scrubbing a picture.
scrubbed.inference: Scrubbing is cleaning so aggressive that the painter's own surface goes too; lifting one added layer a flake at a time under a microscope is slow, targeted work that stops at that layer, and it left the original donors to be seen.

transferred.quote: came home on the same worm-eaten panels
transferred.why: The paint stayed on its original oak, so it was not moved to a new support.
transferred.surface_fit: Old, worm-eaten oak is the classic reason restorers of the 1950s moved paint onto a new backing.
transferred.inference: Transferring lifts the paint off its old support onto a new one; an altarpiece that came home on the same worm-eaten panels still has its paint on the oak it was painted on.

stabilized.quote: with two kneeling donors in the sky where the clouds had been
stabilized.why: The picture now shows figures it did not show before, which is more than securing it.
stabilized.surface_fit: A two-year stay in a restoration workshop for a four-hundred-year-old altarpiece suggests work to keep it from deteriorating further.
stabilized.inference: Stabilizing secures an object in its present state; this altarpiece came back showing donors where clouds had been for two centuries, so its appearance was changed, not merely secured.

worlds.passage: In 1952 a museum sent a sixteenth-century altarpiece, painted on three oak panels and darkened by four centuries of candle smoke and varnish, to a restoration workshop for two years. Because the museum planned a ten-city tour and the three panels together weighed four hundred pounds, the restorers faced the paint with tissue and shaved the sound oak away from behind it. On tour the altarpiece weighed thirty pounds, its back now canvas stretched on aluminum, and crowds saw the same smoke-browned saints they had known in the church. Reviewing the work in 1960, one curator wrote that the restorers had, above all, ______ the altarpiece.
worlds.explanation: The oak was shaved away from behind the paint and the altarpiece's back is now canvas on aluminum, so the restorers "transferred" it to a new support. "Stabilized" fails because the oak was sound; it was removed to save weight for a tour, not to arrest any decay. "Scrubbed" fails because the saints were still smoke-browned, so nothing was cleaned. "Uncovered" fails because the crowds saw the same saints they had always known, so nothing hidden came into view.

stabilized.why: The wood was sound, so the work answered the tour's weight, not any decay.
stabilized.surface_fit: Taking away the wooden backing and giving the paint a new support sounds like structural rescue meant to keep an old painting from falling apart.
stabilized.inference: Stabilizing arrests deterioration in the object as it is; the oak was sound and was taken away because four hundred pounds was too heavy to tour, so the altarpiece was rebuilt on a new support rather than secured on its old one.

scrubbed.why: The smoke was still on the saints, so no cleaning was done.
scrubbed.surface_fit: A centuries-old altarpiece darkened by smoke and varnish is the classic subject of aggressive cleaning by restorers.
scrubbed.inference: Scrubbing is cleaning carried too far; saints still brown with smoke on tour show the surface was not cleaned at all, so there was nothing to have gone too far.

uncovered.quote: they had known in the church
uncovered.why: The crowds saw what they had always seen, so nothing hidden was revealed.
uncovered.surface_fit: Restorers working on a darkened altarpiece are expected to bring hidden detail back into view.
uncovered.inference: Uncovering brings hidden things into view; crowds recognizing the very saints they had known in the church saw nothing new, so whatever the work did, it revealed nothing.

worlds.passage: In 1952 a museum sent a sixteenth-century altarpiece, painted on three oak panels and darkened by four centuries of candle smoke and varnish, to a restoration workshop for two years. The oak had shrunk and split along its grain, lifting the paint into blisters that flaked whenever the heating came on. The restorers laid each blister down with warm wax worked in through the old varnish, and set the panels in a frame that let the wood move; back in church, the congregation noticed only that no flakes fell on the altar cloth. Reviewing the work in 1960, one curator wrote that the restorers had, above all, ______ the altarpiece.
worlds.explanation: Flaking paint was laid back down and the panels framed so the wood could move without cracking the paint, so the restorers "stabilized" the altarpiece. "Transferred" fails because the panels were kept and reframed, so the paint stayed on its oak. "Scrubbed" fails because the wax was worked in through the old varnish, which stayed on. "Uncovered" fails because the congregation noticed nothing different except that the flaking stopped, so nothing hidden came into view.

transferred.quote: set the panels in a frame that let the wood move
transferred.why: The panels were kept as the support, so the paint was not moved to a new one.
transferred.surface_fit: Split, shrinking oak lifting the paint away is exactly the condition that drove restorers of the period to move paint onto a new backing.
transferred.inference: Transferring would take the paint off the failing oak altogether; building a frame that lets the same panels move means the restorers kept the oak as the painting's support.

scrubbed.quote: worked in through the old varnish
scrubbed.why: The varnish was left on and worked through, so the surface was not cleaned.
scrubbed.surface_fit: Two years in a workshop for a smoke-blackened altarpiece suggests heavy cleaning, which is what critics of restorers usually complain of.
scrubbed.inference: Scrubbing strips the surface layers; wax worked in through the old varnish means the varnish was kept as it was, so no layer was stripped.

uncovered.quote: the congregation noticed only that no flakes fell on the altar cloth
uncovered.why: The people who knew it best saw no change in the picture, so nothing was revealed.
uncovered.surface_fit: Restoring a smoke-darkened altarpiece is commonly expected to reveal what the grime has hidden.
uncovered.inference: Uncovering would change what the picture shows; a congregation that saw it every week noticed only that the flaking had stopped, so the image was the same one they had always known.

worlds.passage: In 1952 a museum sent a sixteenth-century altarpiece, painted on three oak panels and darkened by four centuries of candle smoke and varnish, to a restoration workshop for two years. The restorers took the varnish off with strong solvents in weeks, working past the smoke into the paint itself, and in places the thin glazes that had modeled the saints' faces came away on the swabs, leaving flat pink underpaint. The worm holes in the oak, plugged with wax around 1700, were left as they were, and it was hung that spring. Reviewing the work in 1960, one curator wrote that the restorers had, above all, ______ the altarpiece.
worlds.explanation: Strong solvents went past the varnish into the paint and took the glazes off the faces, so the restorers "scrubbed" the altarpiece. "Uncovered" fails because what came off was the painter's own glazes, so the faces lost their modeling and nothing hidden was revealed. "Stabilized" fails because the work removed original paint instead of securing it. "Transferred" fails because the old worm holes in the oak were left as they were, so the paint stayed on its panels.

uncovered.quote: the thin glazes that had modeled the saints' faces came away
uncovered.why: What came off was the painter's own glazes, so nothing hidden was revealed.
uncovered.surface_fit: Taking off centuries of darkened varnish usually shows colors and details no one had seen for generations, which is what uncovering means.
uncovered.inference: Uncovering removes what was laid over the original; here the solvent went past the varnish into the painter's own glazes and left bare underpaint, so the original surface was lost, not revealed.

stabilized.quote: working past the smoke into the paint itself
stabilized.why: The work removed original paint, which is the opposite of securing the picture as it was.
stabilized.surface_fit: A restoration workshop's commission for a fragile old altarpiece suggests conservation work that secures it.
stabilized.inference: Stabilizing preserves the object in its present state; solvents that took the glazes down to the underpaint removed part of the original, so the picture was diminished rather than secured.

transferred.quote: The worm holes in the oak, plugged with wax around 1700, were left as they were
transferred.why: The old oak, worm holes and all, is still the support.
transferred.surface_fit: Moving old paint onto a new backing was a standard 1950s treatment for panel paintings, so it fits a sixteenth-century altarpiece.
transferred.inference: Transferring discards the old support for a new one; worm holes plugged around 1700 still sitting in the oak behind the paint show the panels were never replaced.

topic_tag: a giant planet in a model planetary system
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: One astronomer described the giant as, above all, the system's ______.

worlds.passage: Astronomers modeled a young planetary system with small rocky planets near its star, a belt of icy bodies far out, and a giant planet between them, running the model once with the giant and once without it. With the giant present, icy bodies that drifted near it left on long, stretched paths, three of every four outward and clean out of the system, the fourth inward across the rocky planets' orbits. Within a hundred million years the belt held half as many bodies as in the run without the giant. One astronomer described the giant as, above all, the system's ______.
worlds.explanation: Icy bodies passing near the giant were flung onto stretched paths, most out of the system, so the giant acted as the system's "slingshot." "Umbrella" fails because a quarter of the flung bodies were sent inward across the rocky planets' orbits, so the giant aimed bodies at the inner planets rather than shielding them. "Shepherd" fails because the belt lost half its bodies instead of being kept in bounds. "Tether" fails because the bodies near the giant left on long paths rather than being held in place.

umbrella.quote: the fourth inward across the rocky planets' orbits
umbrella.why: The giant sent some bodies straight toward the inner planets, so it was not shielding them.
umbrella.surface_fit: With half the belt cleared away, fewer icy bodies seem left to threaten the inner planets, and giant planets are often said to shield inner ones.
umbrella.inference: A shield stands between the danger and what it protects and stops what comes; this giant took bodies that were drifting near it and hurled one in four across the rocky planets' orbits, so it was a source of bodies crossing the inner system.

shepherd.quote: the belt held half as many bodies
shepherd.why: The belt lost half its members, so the giant was not keeping it in bounds.
shepherd.surface_fit: A giant planet right next to a belt of small bodies is the classic picture of a planet that herds a belt and holds its edge.
shepherd.inference: A shepherd keeps a belt's bodies inside its bounds; a belt left with half as many bodies as without the giant was being emptied by it, not held together.

tether.why: The bodies near the giant were sent off on long paths, not held near it.
tether.surface_fit: Giant planets do hold small bodies near themselves, so a reader may expect the giant to bind the icy bodies that drift close.
tether.inference: A tether keeps a body bound at one place; bodies that leave the giant's neighborhood on long, stretched paths, most never to return, were released from every hold, the giant's included.

worlds.passage: Astronomers modeled a young planetary system with small rocky planets near its star, a belt of icy bodies far out, and a giant planet between them, running the model once with the giant and once without it. With the giant present, the belt's inner edge stayed sharp for the whole billion years: any icy body that drifted inward toward the giant's orbit was tugged back out within a few thousand circuits, and almost none was lost. Without the giant the belt spread inward into a thin haze, and in both runs the rocky planets were struck about equally often. One astronomer described the giant as, above all, the system's ______.
worlds.explanation: The giant tugged straying bodies back and kept the belt's edge sharp, while without it the belt spread into a haze, so the giant was the system's "shepherd." "Tether" fails because what the giant held was the belt's edge; the bodies themselves kept moving freely within the belt and were never bound to one spot. "Slingshot" fails because almost no body was lost. "Umbrella" fails because the rocky planets were struck about equally often with and without the giant.

tether.quote: the belt's inner edge stayed sharp
tether.why: The giant enforced a boundary for the whole belt rather than holding bodies at a fixed place near itself.
tether.surface_fit: Icy bodies being tugged back whenever they stray sounds like bodies tied on a line to the giant, which is what a tether does.
tether.inference: A tether holds a body at one place; here only straying bodies felt a pull, and only enough to send them back into the belt, where they went on circling freely, so the giant fixed a boundary, not the bodies' positions.

slingshot.why: Hardly any body left, so the giant was not flinging bodies away.
slingshot.surface_fit: Icy bodies falling toward a giant planet are the standard setting for being flung onto new paths by its gravity.
slingshot.inference: A slingshot throws bodies away at speed; bodies near the giant here were tugged back into the belt and almost none was lost, so the giant's pull was keeping them, not hurling them off.

umbrella.quote: in both runs the rocky planets were struck about equally often
umbrella.why: The inner planets were hit as often without the giant, so it protected nothing.
umbrella.surface_fit: A giant standing between the belt and the rocky planets, keeping icy bodies from falling inward, sounds like a shield over the inner system.
umbrella.inference: A shield would cut the impacts on the rocky planets below the rate in the run without it; equal impact rates in both runs mean the inner planets gained nothing from the giant's presence.

worlds.passage: Astronomers modeled a young planetary system with small rocky planets near its star, a belt of icy bodies far out, and a giant planet between them, running the model once with the giant and once without it. With the giant present, the belt fed a steady trickle of icy bodies inward, and nearly every one crossed the giant's path within a few circuits and plunged into its clouds. Over the billion years the rocky planets were struck twenty times less often than in the run without the giant. One astronomer described the giant as, above all, the system's ______.
worlds.explanation: Bodies falling inward toward the rocky planets were caught by the giant, which cut their impacts twentyfold, so the giant served as the system's "umbrella." "Slingshot" fails because the bodies that met the giant plunged into it rather than being flung away. "Shepherd" fails because the belt kept feeding bodies inward, so its bounds were not kept. "Tether" fails because the bodies lasted only a few circuits near the giant instead of being held there.

slingshot.why: The bodies that met the giant fell into it, so it was swallowing bodies, not flinging them.
slingshot.surface_fit: Icy bodies crossing a giant planet's path are the textbook case of being thrown onto new paths by its gravity.
slingshot.inference: A slingshot sends what passes it off at speed; bodies that crossed the giant's path and plunged into its clouds ended inside the giant, so it was taking bodies in, not throwing them away.

shepherd.quote: the belt fed a steady trickle of icy bodies inward
shepherd.why: Bodies kept leaving the belt, so the giant was not holding its edge.
shepherd.surface_fit: A giant planet right next to the belt's inner edge is exactly where a planet that herds a belt would sit.
shepherd.inference: A shepherd keeps a belt in bounds by sending strays back; a belt that kept losing a steady trickle of bodies inward had no one sending them back, and the giant met them only after they had left.

tether.why: The bodies lasted only a few circuits near the giant, so nothing was being held there.
tether.surface_fit: Giant planets do gather small bodies around themselves, so the giant collecting the icy bodies that reach it suggests binding them.
tether.inference: A tether holds a body at a fixed place for good; bodies that met the giant within a few circuits and vanished into it were held for no time at all.

worlds.passage: Astronomers modeled a young planetary system with small rocky planets near its star, a belt of icy bodies far out, and a giant planet between them, running the model once with the giant and once without it. With the giant present, one moon-sized icy body settled into the giant's orbit a sixth of a circuit ahead of it and, for a billion years, swung back and forth around that point, never straying more than a few degrees. Bodies falling inward crossed the giant's orbit unhindered, and the belt thinned into the same haze as without the giant. One astronomer described the giant as, above all, the system's ______.
worlds.explanation: One body was held at a fixed point ahead of the giant for a billion years, swinging around that point but never leaving it, so the giant served as the system's "tether." "Shepherd" fails because the belt thinned into the same haze as without the giant, so the giant held no group in bounds; it held one body at one point. "Umbrella" fails because bodies falling inward crossed the giant's orbit unhindered. "Slingshot" fails because the body near the giant stayed within a few degrees of one point for a billion years.

shepherd.quote: thinned into the same haze as without the giant
shepherd.why: The giant made no difference to the belt, so it was not herding any group of bodies.
shepherd.surface_fit: A giant keeping an icy body in order on its own orbit for a billion years sounds like a planet that herds the small bodies around it.
shepherd.inference: A shepherd keeps a whole population in bounds; a belt that thinned exactly as it did without the giant shows the giant herded nothing, and what it held was a single body at a single point.

umbrella.why: Bodies falling toward the inner planets passed the giant freely, so it shielded nothing.
umbrella.surface_fit: A giant planet standing between the belt and the rocky planets looks like a shield over the inner system.
umbrella.inference: A shield stops what comes toward the thing it protects; bodies trickling inward from the belt crossed the giant's orbit unhindered on their way to the inner system, so the giant stopped none of them.

slingshot.quote: never straying more than a few degrees
