plowed.surface_fit: A brown, fast flood off burned hills sounds violent, and saying it plowed the fields is a natural way to describe a flood that churned farmland.
plowed.inference: Last year's rows were still there to drill into beneath the silt, so the old surface stayed in place and the silt was laid on top of it.

worlds.passage: In the spring of 1952 a river in a dry farming valley flooded the lower fields, where irrigation had left a pale crust of salt. The water came down from the upland meadows and ran off the hard crust within a day; cattle grazed last year's stubble that autumn. Next spring the fallow fields came up thick with wild rye and bluestem, grasses the valley had only on those meadows. On the sown ones, the same seed wheat yielded half as much as on the upper slopes, as it always had. In a report on the valley's farms, one soil scientist wrote that the flood had ______ the lower fields.
worlds.explanation: The water came from the upland meadows, and the next spring the unsown lower fields grew grasses that the valley had only on those meadows, so the flood "reseeded" the fields. "Rinsed" fails because the water ran off the hard crust within a day and the wheat still yielded half as much, so the salt stayed. "Replenished" fails because the sown wheat yielded no better than it always had, and "plowed" fails because cattle still grazed the old stubble.

rinsed.quote: ran off the hard crust within a day
rinsed.why: The water ran off the crust instead of soaking through it, and the wheat still yielded half as much, so the salt was not washed out.
rinsed.surface_fit: The fields were salt-crusted and a flood crossed them, so "the flood had rinsed the lower fields" is the natural first guess for what water did to salty ground.
rinsed.inference: Water that runs off a hard crust in a day never passes down through the soil, and the sown wheat stayed at half the upland yield, which is what salt left in place does; so nothing was rinsed out.

replenished.quote: yielded half as much as on the upper slopes, as it always had
replenished.why: The sown wheat grew no better than before, so the flood added nothing to the soil's fertility.
replenished.surface_fit: The fields burst into thick growth the spring after the flood, and floods are commonly said to replenish farmland, so the word fits both the sentence and the topic.
replenished.inference: If the flood had enriched the soil, the wheat sown on those same lower fields would have yielded more; it yielded what it always had, so the thick new growth came from new plants arriving, not richer ground.

plowed.why: The old stubble was still there to graze, so the surface was never torn or turned.
plowed.surface_fit: New plants springing up in fallow ground suggests the ground was broken open, and a flood that plowed fields is an ordinary phrase.
plowed.inference: Stubble left standing to graze means the soil around it was not cut or turned over; the new grasses grew on an undisturbed surface.

worlds.passage: In the spring of 1952 a river in a dry farming valley flooded the lower fields, where irrigation had left a pale crust of salt. The water burst through a failed levee in a current strong enough to roll boulders and was gone within hours. Behind it last year's stubble had vanished, the crust lay broken into slabs turned on edge, and the pale sand from beneath it was heaped in long ridges running downstream, with furrows scoured between them. The farmers then sowed the same seed wheat into the furrows. In a report on the valley's farms, one soil scientist wrote that the flood had ______ the lower fields.
worlds.explanation: The stubble was gone, the crust was broken and turned on edge, and the sand beneath lay in ridges and furrows that the farmers sowed straight into, so the flood "plowed" the lower fields. "Rinsed" fails because the water was gone within hours and the salt crust was still there, only broken into slabs. "Replenished" fails because the ridges were the sand from under the crust, and "reseeded" fails because the farmers sowed their same seed wheat.

rinsed.quote: the crust lay broken into slabs
rinsed.why: The salt crust was still lying on the fields in broken slabs, and the water had passed in hours, so the salt was not washed away.
rinsed.surface_fit: A flood crossing salt-crusted ground and breaking up the crust looks like it cleaned the fields, so rinsed is a tempting reading of what the water did.
rinsed.inference: The salt was still present in slabs on the surface, and water gone within hours has no time to soak down through the soil and carry salt away, so the crust was broken up, not washed out.

replenished.quote: the pale sand from beneath it
replenished.why: The ridges were the sand from under the crust, so the flood moved the fields' own soil rather than adding any.
replenished.surface_fit: Ridges of heaped soil after a flood look like a fresh deposit, and floods are commonly said to replenish fields with new earth.
replenished.inference: The heaped material was the pale sand from beneath the crust, the fields' own soil turned up and rearranged; new soil brought by the water would be silt from upstream laid on top.

reseeded.quote: sowed the same seed wheat into the furrows
reseeded.why: The farmers planted their own seed into the furrows the water made, so the flood supplied the ground, not the seed.
reseeded.surface_fit: Furrowed ground ready for sowing suggests a new start for the fields, and floods that leave seeds behind are said to reseed them.
reseeded.inference: The crop came from the farmers' own seed sown into the new furrows; the flood's work was on the shape of the ground, which is what plowing does before sowing.

topic_tag: a hill temple and a city temple
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: One architectural historian concludes that the hill temple is best understood as the city temple's ______.

worlds.passage: A great stone temple was finished in a river city in 1580; a smaller wooden temple stands on a hill a day's walk north. Its four shrines stand in the city temple's order, and the dragons over its gate match the city temple's at a third the size. One of them even repeats the chipped claw that a city carver left by accident on his dragon. Farming families built it, take turns sweeping it, and still walk to the city each spring for the great festival. One architectural historian concludes that the hill temple is best understood as the city temple's ______.
worlds.explanation: The hill temple repeats the city temple's shrine order and gate carvings at a third the size, even copying a chip a city carver made by accident, so it is the city temple's "replica". "Precursor" fails because copying that accidental chip means the hill carver worked from the finished city dragon. "Offshoot" fails because farming families built and keep it, and "rival" fails because they still walk to the city festival every spring.

precursor.quote: the chipped claw that a city carver left by accident
precursor.why: The hill temple reproduces a slip made by the city temple's own carver, which it could only have taken from the city temple, so the copying ran from city to hill.
precursor.surface_fit: An old wooden temple on a hill that shares the great temple's plan looks like the original the city builders worked from, so precursor is the natural first guess.
precursor.inference: An accident belongs to the carving it happened on; a chip a city carver made by mistake can appear on the hill dragon only if the hill carver was copying the finished city dragon, so the hill temple came after the city temple and cannot be its forerunner.

offshoot.quote: Farming families built it, take turns sweeping it
offshoot.why: Local farmers built and keep the temple, so it was not founded by a group from the city temple.
offshoot.surface_fit: A smaller temple of the same pattern a day's walk away sounds like a branch planted by the city temple, and offshoot is a normal word for a daughter house.
offshoot.inference: An offshoot grows out of the parent itself, its own people setting up elsewhere; a temple built and swept by farming families came from the villagers, and what it took from the city was only a design.

rival.quote: still walk to the city each spring
rival.why: Its own keepers still go to the city temple's festival, so it draws no worshippers away.
rival.surface_fit: A second temple near a famous one could easily be competing with it, and historians often call such a building a rival.
rival.inference: A rival pulls worshippers away; the families who built the hill temple still make the yearly walk to the city festival, so the two temples serve the same people.

worlds.passage: A great stone temple was finished in a river city in 1580; a smaller wooden temple stands on a hill a day's walk north. Rings in its oldest beams date them to the 1490s. Its four shrines stand in the city temple's order, and the dragons over the city temple's gate match its own, scale for scale, at three times the size. Records name the city temple's builder as a carpenter on the hill in his youth. Its farming families still walk to the city each spring for the great festival. One architectural historian concludes that the hill temple is best understood as the city temple's ______.
worlds.explanation: The hill temple's beams date to the 1490s, its plan and carvings reappear in the city temple at three times the size, and the city temple's builder worked on the hill as a young man, so the hill temple is the city temple's "precursor". "Replica" fails because the hill temple is ninety years older and cannot copy a temple not yet built. "Offshoot" fails because influence ran from the hill to the city, and "rival" fails because its families still walk to the city festival.

replica.why: The hill temple is ninety years older than the city temple, so it cannot be a copy of it.
replica.surface_fit: The two temples share a shrine order and carved dragons, one at a third the size of the other, which is exactly what makes a small building look like a replica of a great one.
replica.inference: A copy has to come after its original; timber cut in the 1490s means the hill temple stood ninety years before the city temple was finished, so the matching design was carried from the hill to the city, not the other way.

offshoot.quote: a carpenter on the hill in his youth
offshoot.why: The city temple's builder learned on the hill, so the city temple grew out of the hill temple, the reverse of an offshoot.
offshoot.surface_fit: Two temples with one plan, linked by a builder who worked on both, sound like a parent temple and a daughter house, and offshoot names that kind of relation.
offshoot.inference: An offshoot grows from the parent and comes after it; here the hill temple is older and the city temple's builder trained there, so if either grew out of the other, the city temple grew out of the hill temple.

rival.quote: still walk to the city each spring
rival.why: The hill temple's families take part in the city festival, so the hill temple is not competing with the city temple.
rival.surface_fit: An older temple whose design was taken for a grander one might resent or compete with it, and rival is an ordinary word for a neighboring temple.
rival.inference: Competition would show as worshippers kept away from the city; instead the hill temple's own families go to the city festival every year, so the relation is one of descent in design, not contest.

worlds.passage: A great stone temple was finished in a river city in 1580; a smaller wooden temple stands on a hill a day's walk north. In 1608 a dispute over the festival calendar split the city temple's monks, and the smaller party, wanting the great festival at harvest rather than in spring, walked north and built on the hill. Its two shrines stand side by side under thatch like the farmhouses around them, and each new head of the hill temple still travels to the city to be confirmed by its abbot. One architectural historian concludes that the hill temple is best understood as the city temple's ______.
worlds.explanation: Part of the city temple's own monks broke away and built on the hill, and each new head is still confirmed by the city abbot, so the hill temple is the city temple's "offshoot". "Rival" fails because a temple whose heads the city abbot confirms remains under the city temple. "Replica" fails because its thatched shrines look like the farmhouses around them, and "precursor" fails because it was built by monks who had come from the city temple.

rival.quote: travels to the city to be confirmed by its abbot
rival.why: The hill temple's head is still confirmed by the city abbot, so the hill temple remains under the city temple.
rival.surface_fit: The hill temple was founded after a dispute split the city's monks, and a breakaway temple after a quarrel is the natural setting for rival.
rival.inference: A rival is independent of the temple it competes with; a temple whose every head must be confirmed by the city abbot is still governed from the city, and its harvest festival does not compete for the spring crowds.

replica.quote: under thatch like the farmhouses around them
replica.why: The hill temple is built like the local farmhouses, so it does not reproduce the city temple's design.
replica.surface_fit: A temple founded by the city temple's own monks would be expected to copy the great temple they came from, so replica tempts.
replica.inference: A replica reproduces the original's design; two thatched shrines like the farmhouses around them are nothing like a great stone temple, so the monks took their community north but not the building.

precursor.quote: walked north and built on the hill
precursor.why: The hill temple was built by monks who had left the city temple, so the city temple was already standing.
precursor.surface_fit: A wooden hill temple next to a stone city temple looks like the older, simpler form the great temple developed from.
precursor.inference: Its builders were monks of the city temple who split off and walked north, so the city temple had to exist, with its monks and its festival, before the hill temple did; a forerunner comes first, and this temple came out of the city temple.

worlds.passage: A great stone temple was finished in a river city in 1580; a smaller wooden temple stands on a hill a day's walk north. A lord of the northern hills built it, and its monks came from a coastal order and kept that order's rule. He set its festival for the same spring week as the city's, beneath a gate carved taller than the city temple's. Within ten years the city's festival tolls had fallen by half. One architectural historian concludes that the hill temple is best understood as the city temple's ______.
worlds.explanation: A hill lord built the temple with monks of another order, set its festival for the city's own spring week, and within ten years the city's festival tolls had fallen by half, so it was the city temple's "rival". "Offshoot" fails because its monks came from a coastal order with its own rule. "Replica" fails because its gate was carved taller than the city temple's, and "precursor" fails because its festival was timed against a city festival already being held.

offshoot.quote: came from a coastal order and kept that order's rule
offshoot.why: Its monks belonged to a different order, so the hill temple did not grow out of the city temple's community.
offshoot.surface_fit: A temple founded a day's walk from the city temple sounds like a daughter house, which is what offshoot names.
offshoot.inference: An offshoot's founders come out of the parent; these monks came from a coastal order and followed its rule, and the builder was a hill lord, so nothing of the city temple went into founding it.

replica.why: The hill temple's gate was made bigger than the city temple's, not a scaled copy of it.
replica.surface_fit: A temple built near a famous one, in the same years and with the same festival, could easily be a copy of it, and replica fits a smaller building beside a great one.
replica.inference: A replica reproduces its original, usually smaller; a gate deliberately carved taller than the city temple's is built to outdo the city temple, not to reproduce it.

precursor.quote: for the same spring week as the city's
precursor.why: The hill festival was timed to the city's existing festival week, so the city temple was already there to compete with.
precursor.surface_fit: A modest wooden temple on a hill seems older than a great stone one in a city, so precursor is a natural first guess.
precursor.inference: A festival set to fall in the same week as the city's is set against a festival already being held; and the city's tolls fell afterward, so the hill temple arrived when the city temple was established, and cannot be the earlier building it followed.

topic_tag: winter sea ice in a northern bay
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: One marine biologist has written that the bay's winter ice serves its animals above all as their ______.

worlds.passage: Each winter ice covers much of a northern bay where seals, seabirds, cod, and krill live. The ice there breaks into floes that drift south with the current. Harp seal pups are born on the floes late in winter and cannot swim for their first two weeks, and by the time they can, the floes have drifted a hundred miles south, to the shoals where young seals feed. The floes are thick and snow-covered, and almost nothing grows beneath them. One marine biologist has written that the bay's winter ice serves its animals above all as their ______.
worlds.explanation: The seal pups are born on drifting floes and cannot swim for two weeks, by which time the floes have carried them a hundred miles to their feeding shoals, so the ice serves as their "raft". "Perch" fails because the pups cannot leave the floe while it travels. "Pantry" fails because almost nothing grows under the thick, snowy floes, and "roof" fails because the seals live on top of the ice.

perch.quote: cannot swim for their first two weeks
perch.why: The pups cannot leave the floe and stay on it while it travels, so it is not a stopping place between trips.
perch.surface_fit: Seals lying out on ice are a familiar picture, and calling the ice the animals' perch is a natural way to describe a place they rest on.
perch.inference: A perch is a fixed spot an animal lands on between trips out; these pups cannot leave the floe for two weeks while it moves a hundred miles, so what matters is that the ice carries them.

pantry.why: Thick, snow-covered floes grow almost nothing underneath, and the pups are nursing, so the ice supplies no food.
pantry.surface_fit: Sea ice is well known as a source of food for polar animals, so pantry fits both the sentence and a passage about seals on ice.
pantry.inference: The floes are too thick and snowy to grow anything beneath them, and the pups feed on milk while aboard and then at the shoals they reach; the food is at the destination, and the ice is what gets them there.

roof.why: The seals live on top of the floes, so the ice is not covering them.
roof.surface_fit: An ice sheet over a bay covers the water like a roof, and a biologist could describe it as sheltering the bay's animals.
roof.inference: A roof shelters what is beneath it; the pups that depend on this ice are born and lie on its top, exposed, so the ice is useful as something that bears and moves them.

worlds.passage: Each winter ice covers much of a northern bay where seals, seabirds, cod, and krill live. The ice there is thin and clear, and algae grow all winter in the brine channels inside it. In spring, as the ice melts, the algae spill into the water, and krill swarm at the melting edge to eat them weeks before any plankton blooms in open water, with cod and ringed seals hunting close behind. When the last floes drift out to sea, the krill stay behind. One marine biologist has written that the bay's winter ice serves its animals above all as their ______.
worlds.explanation: Algae grow all winter inside the ice and spill out as it melts, feeding the krill weeks before any plankton blooms, with cod and seals following, so the ice serves as the animals' "pantry". "Roof" fails because the krill gather where the ice is melting away. "Raft" fails because the krill stay behind when the floes drift off, and "perch" fails because the seals are hunting in the water, not resting on the ice.

roof.why: The krill gather where the ice is melting away, so they come for what it releases, not for cover.
roof.surface_fit: Krill living around sea ice suggests the ice is sheltering them, and roof is a natural word for ice covering small animals in a bay.
roof.inference: A roof is valuable while it stands over its occupants; the krill swarm at the edge as the ice melts and disappears, and their hunters follow them there, so the ice matters for the algae it holds.

raft.why: When the ice drifts away the krill do not go with it, so it never carried them.
raft.surface_fit: The ice breaks up and drifts out to sea with animals around it, and raft is the stock image for floating ice animals travel with.
raft.inference: If the ice mattered to the krill as a carrier they would leave with it; they stay behind, so they were there for the algae the ice stored and let go as it melted.

perch.why: The seals hunt in the water behind the krill, so they are not resting on the ice.
perch.surface_fit: Seals are well known for hauling out on ice, so perch fits a passage about seals and sea ice.
perch.inference: A perch is somewhere an animal rests out of the water; these seals are in the water chasing the cod and krill at the melting edge, so the ice draws them through the food it releases.

worlds.passage: Each winter ice covers much of a northern bay where seals, seabirds, cod, and krill live. The ice there is frozen fast to the shore, thick and snow-covered, so the water beneath stays dark and almost nothing grows there. Young cod spend the winter in crevices on its underside, swimming out at night to feed in open water past its edge. The seabirds that hunt them find fish by sight, and at the bay's mouth, where no ice forms, they take most of the young cod wintering there. One marine biologist has written that the bay's winter ice serves its animals above all as their ______.
worlds.explanation: Young cod hide in crevices under the dark ice by day, and the seabirds that hunt by sight take most of the young cod only at the ice-free mouth of the bay, so the ice serves as the cod's "roof". "Pantry" fails because almost nothing grows under the thick, snowy ice and the cod swim out past its edge to feed. "Raft" fails because the ice is frozen fast to the shore and carries nothing, and "perch" fails because the cod live under the ice, not on it.

pantry.quote: swimming out at night to feed
pantry.why: The cod leave the ice to feed in open water, and almost nothing grows under it, so the ice is not their food source.
pantry.surface_fit: Fish crowding under sea ice for the whole winter suggests they are feeding there, and pantry is a familiar word for sea ice in polar biology.
pantry.inference: The water under thick, snow-covered ice stays dark, so nothing grows to eat, and the cod swim past the ice edge at night to feed; they spend the day under the ice for some reason other than food.

raft.why: Ice fixed to the shore does not move, so it cannot carry the animals anywhere.
raft.surface_fit: Floating sea ice is often described as carrying animals across polar waters, so raft fits a passage about animals and winter ice.
raft.inference: Shore-fast ice stays where it is all winter, so it takes nothing anywhere; and the cod are under it, not on it.

perch.why: The cod live in the ice's underside, so the ice is not a place they stand on between trips.
perch.surface_fit: Seabirds appear in the passage, and seabirds are known for resting on ice near the water they fish, so perch tempts on a first read.
perch.inference: A perch is something an animal stands on; the animals the ice protects here are cod tucked into crevices beneath it, and the birds are their hunters, which the ice keeps away from them.

worlds.passage: Each winter ice covers much of a northern bay where seals, seabirds, cod, and krill live. Along the shore the ice is frozen fast to the shallow bottom, thick and snow-covered. Past its edge a lane of open water stays clear, and eiders and guillemots stand in rows along the edge between dives, plunging into the lane after fish. On the few days when gales pack the lane with drifting ice, the birds leave the bay. One marine biologist has written that the bay's winter ice serves its animals above all as their ______.
worlds.explanation: Eiders and guillemots stand on the fixed ice edge between dives into the open lane, and they leave the bay when the lane closes, so the ice serves as their "perch". "Raft" fails because this ice is frozen fast to the bottom. "Pantry" fails because the birds catch their fish in the open lane, and "roof" fails because nothing lives under ice frozen to the bottom; the birds stand on top.

raft.quote: frozen fast to the shallow bottom
raft.why: Ice frozen to the bottom cannot drift, so it carries the birds nowhere.
raft.surface_fit: Birds standing in rows on ice look like passengers, and raft is a common image for polar animals riding ice.
raft.inference: A raft matters because it floats and moves; ice frozen fast to the bottom stays put all winter, so it gives the birds a place to stand beside the open water.

pantry.quote: plunging into the lane after fish
pantry.why: The birds catch their food in the open lane, not from the ice.
pantry.surface_fit: The birds feed at the ice all winter, and pantry is a familiar way to describe ice that supports polar animals' feeding.
pantry.inference: The fish are in the open lane; ice frozen to the shallow bottom has no water beneath it for anything to grow in, and when gales close the lane the birds leave though the ice remains, so the ice was only a stand next to the food.

roof.quote: stand in rows along the edge
roof.why: The birds stand on top of the ice, so it does not shelter them from above.
roof.surface_fit: Ice over a bay covers the water like a roof, and a biologist could describe it as sheltering the bay's animals.
roof.inference: A roof shelters what is under it; this ice is frozen to the bottom, so nothing lives under it, and the birds that use it stand exposed on its top.

topic_tag: a summer drought on a trout river
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: In a report on that summer, one hydrologist wrote that the drought had ______ the river.

worlds.passage: In 1976 almost no rain fell for eleven summer weeks on a trout river that runs twenty miles from upland springs to a lake. By the eighth week the gauge halfway down read no flow at all, and the gravel riffles between the river's deep bends lay exposed. The bends, fed by seepage from shaded hillsides, kept their depth, and trout tagged in one bend that summer were never caught in the next, though biologists found them crowded ten times thicker than in spring. Nearly all were alive when the autumn rains came. In a report on that summer, one hydrologist wrote that the drought had ______ the river.
worlds.explanation: The flow stopped and the riffles lay exposed, while the bends kept their depth and held crowded trout that never moved between them, so the drought "pooled" the river. "Pinched" fails because the trout could not pass from bend to bend. "Parched" fails because the bends kept their depth, and "overheated" fails because the crowded trout survived.

pinched.why: Trout could not pass from one bend to the next, so no stream still connected them.
pinched.surface_fit: A river shrinking in a drought is commonly described as pinched, and exposed gravel makes that the first picture a reader forms.
pinched.inference: A pinched river is a narrowed but continuous stream that fish can travel; trout that never reached the next bend all summer were held in separate bodies of water.

parched.why: Water stayed deep in the bends all summer, so the river was not dried out.
parched.surface_fit: Eleven rainless weeks and dry white gravel in the sun are the classic image of a drought-parched river, so the word fits both the sentence and the scene.
parched.inference: The bends were fed by seepage and kept their depth, so the river still held water along its length in separate bodies; parched would mean the bed itself had gone dry.

overheated.why: Crowded trout survived the summer, which they could not do in water that had grown too warm.
overheated.surface_fit: Trout crowded into still water under a summer sun are exactly what an overheated river kills, so overheated tempts.
overheated.inference: Trout die when water warms past what they tolerate, and crowding makes it worse; these crowded trout lived, so the seepage from shaded hillsides kept the bends cool.

worlds.passage: In 1976 almost no rain fell for eleven summer weeks on a trout river that runs twenty miles from upland springs to a lake. By the eighth week the flow at the gauge halfway down had fallen to a fifth of its usual summer level, and the mill where the river meets the lake turned its wheel, slowly, every day of the summer. Anglers could step across the river at any riffle, and trout tagged in one bend were caught in others all summer. Nearly all were alive when the autumn rains came. In a report on that summer, one hydrologist wrote that the drought had ______ the river.
worlds.explanation: The flow fell to a fifth but kept the mill wheel turning, anglers could step across at any riffle, and trout still moved from bend to bend, so the drought "pinched" the river. "Pooled" fails because the trout moved between the bends. "Parched" fails because the mill wheel turned every day, and "overheated" fails because nearly all the trout survived.

pooled.why: Trout traveled between bends all summer, so the bends stayed joined by running water.
pooled.surface_fit: A drought river with deep bends and riffles is often left as a chain of pools, so pooled is a strong first guess.
pooled.inference: Pools are separate bodies of standing water; trout moving from bend to bend all summer means a stream still ran over every riffle and connected them.

parched.quote: turned its wheel, slowly, every day
parched.why: Water reached the mill at the lake every day, so the river never ran dry.
parched.surface_fit: Eleven rainless weeks and a river anglers could step across sound like a drought-parched river, a stock phrase.
parched.inference: A mill wheel turns only on moving water; the wheel at the river's mouth turned every day, so water came down the whole river all summer.

overheated.why: The trout survived, so the shrunken stream did not grow too warm for them.
overheated.surface_fit: A shallow stream in an eleven-week drought would be expected to warm, and an overheated river is a familiar drought story.
overheated.inference: Trout are the first to die when a river warms; nearly all of them lived, so whatever the drought did to this river, it did not raise the water past what trout can stand.

worlds.passage: In 1976 almost no rain fell for eleven summer weeks on a trout river that runs twenty miles from upland springs to a lake. Its springs held up, and in the eighth week the mill where the river meets the lake still turned its wheel at its usual summer speed. Along the shallow, treeless lower miles, biologists counted thousands of dead trout, many carrying tags put on near the springs that spring. In the shaded upper miles near the cold springs, the trout lived. In a report on that summer, one hydrologist wrote that the drought had ______ the river.
worlds.explanation: The river kept its usual flow, yet trout died by the thousands in the shallow, treeless lower miles while they lived in the shaded miles near the cold springs, so the drought "overheated" the river. "Pooled" fails because tagged trout traveled from the springs downstream. "Pinched" fails because the mill turned at its usual speed, and "parched" fails because the springs held up.

pooled.quote: carrying tags put on near the springs
pooled.why: Trout tagged at the springs reached the lower miles, so the river was still connected from end to end.
pooled.surface_fit: Fish surviving only in a few places along a drought river suggests they were stranded in pools, and pooled is the usual word for that.

repopulated.quote: moved on to a strike farther north

worlds.passage: In 1897 gold was found in the hills above a small river town, and the rush lasted six years. "Ruined" fails because the reopened school shows a growing town, and "reoriented" fails because the new farmers shipped from the old river landing.

overran.why: The miners moved into houses the shrunken town had left empty, so they fit into room the town already had.
overran.surface_fit: A rush of miners into a small town is the classic picture of a town overrun, so the word fits both the sentence and the topic.
overran.inference: Overrunning means swamping a place beyond what it can hold; this town had lost four fifths of its people and the miners rented houses already standing empty, then stayed on as farmers.

ruined.inference: A school reopens only when there are children to fill it again; one shut since 1885 needing three teachers by 1920 means families had come to live in the town, the opposite of ruin.

overran.quote: The diggings lay a day's ride away

repopulated.surface_fit: Gold rushes drew thousands of people to new places, and a historian could naturally say one repopulated a small town.
repopulated.inference: Repopulating would bring lasting residents; farms turned into a timber company's pine plantation hold trees instead of farming families, so the town lost households.

topic_tag: a copper mountain after mining

worlds.passage: For eighty years after 1890, companies mined copper from a mountain above a valley town, until the last mine closed in 1972. worlds.explanation: All the ore left through one mine head, the forest and the mountain's height are unchanged, and the ground has been sinking and splitting on three sides, so mining had "riddled" the mountain with workings. "Pitted" fails because the forest is unbroken on every slope. "Razed" fails because the mountain still shades the town until nine, and "poisoned" fails because the town still drinks from its streams.

pitted.why: The slopes carry unbroken forest, so no holes were dug into the surface.
pitted.surface_fit: Ground dropping and a spring vanishing into the ground sound like a pitted surface, and pitted is a common word for land marked by mining.
pitted.inference: Open pits break the forest wherever they are dug; unbroken forest on every slope and one mine head for all the ore mean the ground is sinking into spaces cut beneath it, not into holes dug from above.

razed.quote: keeps the morning sun off the town until nine
razed.why: The mountain still casts the town's morning shadow, so it has kept its height.

poisoned.inference: A town does not keep drinking from streams fouled by mine waste; drawing its water from them still means the runoff is clean, so what mining harmed is the ground's support.

riddled.surface_fit: Mining a dozen separate ore bodies in one mountain sounds like it would leave the mountain full of workings, which is what riddled describes.
riddled.inference: Riddled means pierced with passages; miners who worked in daylight for eighty years were digging from the surface, so they left craters, not tunnels.

razed.quote: keeps the morning sun off the town until nine
razed.why: The mountain still shades the town in the morning, so its height is unchanged.
razed.surface_fit: Open-pit mining strips away the land, and a geologist could easily say eighty years of it razed a mountain.
razed.inference: If the mountain had been leveled, the morning sun would reach the town sooner; it does not, so the digging was confined to scattered pockets on its slopes.

poisoned.inference: Trout cannot be raised in water carrying mine waste; a hatchery still using the mountain's streams means the craters marked the land without fouling its water.

"Riddled" fails because the miners worked in daylight from the top down, and "poisoned" fails because a trout hatchery still uses its water.

pitted.quote: one great body under the summit
pitted.why: The ore was a single mass under the top, so taking it removed the top as a whole rather than leaving scattered holes.
pitted.surface_fit: Mining from the surface with the rock carried away is how open pits are made, so pitted is the natural first guess.

riddled.quote: a single shaft from one deep vein

riddled.surface_fit: Old copper workings suggest a mountain full of tunnels, and riddled is the usual word for that.

topic_tag: a century of a small country's wheat duty
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Surveying that century, one economist calls the duty a kind of ______.

worlds.passage: From 1850 to 1950 a small country taxed every bushel of wheat brought in through its ports, and the rate changed eleven times. Each change came in a year when wheat prices had slumped, and each time farm members won it by pointing to the higher duties already charged next door. In the good years that followed, bills to lower the duty always failed, and by 1950 it stood at nine times its first level. Surveying that century, one economist calls the duty a kind of ______.
worlds.explanation: Every change raised the duty in a slump, no good year brought it down, and it climbed to nine times its first level, so it was a "ratchet". "Pendulum" fails because the duty never swung back. "Regulator" fails because it was not cut when prices recovered, and "pacemaker" fails because each rise followed higher duties already charged next door.

pendulum.quote: bills to lower the duty always failed
pendulum.why: The duty was never brought back down, so it never swung back.
pendulum.surface_fit: A duty changed eleven times over a century and fought over in good years and bad sounds like it swung back and forth.
pendulum.inference: A pendulum swings both ways around a center; with every attempt to lower the duty failing and the duty ending at nine times its first level, it moved in one direction only.

regulator.quote: In the good years that followed
regulator.why: The duty was raised in slumps but left high in good years, so it did not steady prices in both directions.
regulator.surface_fit: The duty went up whenever wheat prices slumped, which is exactly how a stabilizing tariff behaves, so regulator is a strong first reading.
regulator.inference: A regulator corrects both ways, cutting the duty when prices recover; in the good years after each rise the duty stayed put, so each slump only added to it.

pacemaker.quote: the higher duties already charged next door
pacemaker.why: The neighbors' duties were already higher, so this country was following them, not setting the pace.
pacemaker.surface_fit: A small country raising its grain duty again and again could plausibly be leading its neighbors, and pacemaker fits a tariff others follow.
pacemaker.inference: A pacemaker moves first and others follow; each rise here was argued for by pointing at duties already higher next door, so this country was catching up.

worlds.passage: From 1850 to 1950 a small country taxed every bushel of wheat brought in through its ports, and the rate changed eleven times. In 1950 the rate stood within a cent of its first level, while the neighboring countries kept their 1850 duties throughout. Surveying that century, one economist calls the duty a kind of ______.
worlds.explanation: The duty rose under one party and fell under the other as they traded office, ending within a cent of where it began, so it was a "pendulum". "Ratchet" fails because the duty came back to its starting level. "Regulator" fails because two rises came in years of record prices, and "pacemaker" fails because the neighbors kept their 1850 duties throughout.

ratchet.quote: within a cent of its first level
ratchet.why: After a century of changes the duty was back where it began, so it did not climb one way.
ratchet.surface_fit: A grain duty pushed up by a farm party again and again sounds like it could only climb, which is what ratchet describes.
ratchet.inference: A ratchet keeps every rise; a duty that ended within a cent of its starting level gave back each rise in a later cut, as the parties traded office.

regulator.quote: Two of the rises came in years of record wheat prices
regulator.why: The duty went up when wheat was already dear, which would push prices higher, not steady them.
regulator.surface_fit: A duty that rose and fell over the century looks like it was being adjusted to keep wheat prices steady, so regulator is tempting.
regulator.inference: A regulator raises the duty when prices are low and cuts it when they are high; rises in record-price years mean the changes followed which party held office, not what wheat cost.

pacemaker.why: The neighbors never changed their duties, so none of them followed this country's.
pacemaker.surface_fit: A small country whose tariff moved often could set the pattern for its neighbors, and pacemaker fits a duty that changed eleven times.
pacemaker.inference: A pacemaker is followed; the neighbors kept their 1850 duties for the whole century while this one rose and fell, so its swings set no pace for anyone.

worlds.passage: From 1850 to 1950 a small country taxed every bushel of wheat brought in through its ports, and the rate changed eleven times. A law of 1850 raised the rate whenever wheat at the capital's exchange fell below one price and cut it whenever wheat rose above another, and all eleven changes, five of them cuts, followed that law under whichever party governed. Over the century, wheat prices there moved half as much as in the neighboring countries, whose duties were set by their own parliaments' votes. Surveying that century, one economist calls the duty a kind of ______.
worlds.explanation: By law the duty rose when wheat was cheap and fell when it was dear, every change followed that law whatever party governed, and wheat prices moved half as much as next door, so the duty was a "regulator". "Ratchet" fails because five of the changes were cuts. "Pendulum" fails because the changes followed prices, not the party in office, and "pacemaker" fails because the neighbors set their duties by their own votes.

ratchet.why: The duty fell five times, so it was not a one-way climb.
ratchet.surface_fit: The duty rose automatically every time wheat fell below a set price, which sounds like a mechanism that keeps pushing it up, as a ratchet does.
ratchet.inference: A ratchet holds every gain; this duty was cut whenever wheat rose above the upper price, five times in all, so it moved down as readily as up.

pendulum.why: The changes followed the law's price marks no matter who was in office, so they did not swing with politics.
pendulum.surface_fit: A duty that went up and down repeatedly over a century looks like it swung back and forth, and pendulum is the stock image for a policy that keeps reversing.
pendulum.inference: A pendulum swings on its own rhythm between two sides; these rises and cuts came whenever wheat crossed the law's two prices, under any government, so they tracked the market rather than alternating.

pacemaker.quote: set by their own parliaments' votes
pacemaker.why: The neighbors chose their duties by their own votes and their prices swung twice as much, so they were not copying this country's rule.
pacemaker.surface_fit: A small country with a clever automatic duty could plausibly have set the pattern for its neighbors, and pacemaker fits a tariff others copy.
pacemaker.inference: If the neighbors had followed this duty, their prices would have steadied too; they set their duties by vote and their wheat prices moved twice as much, so the law kept prices steady at home without leading anyone.

Surveying that century, one economist calls the duty a kind of ______.
worlds.explanation: Within two years of every change the three neighbors set their duties to match, and traders in all four countries quoted wheat at this country's rate, so the duty was a "pacemaker". "Ratchet" fails because the duty ended at half its first level. "Pendulum" fails because after three rises it only fell, and "regulator" fails because the changes paid for the navy, not steadied wheat prices.

ratchet.quote: by 1950 the rate was half its first level
ratchet.why: The duty ended lower than it began, so it did not climb one way.
ratchet.surface_fit: A tariff that the neighbors kept having to match sounds like one that kept ratcheting up, and ratchet is a familiar word for a duty that is hard to lower.
ratchet.inference: A ratchet holds every gain; this duty gave back all its rises and more, ending at half its first level, so it could move down as easily as up.

pendulum.quote: falling at each of the eight later cuts
pendulum.why: After three rises the duty only fell, so it did not swing back and forth.
pendulum.surface_fit: A duty that rose and then fell over a century sounds like it swung, and pendulum is the stock image for a policy that keeps reversing.
pendulum.inference: A pendulum keeps swinging back through the center; this duty rose three times and then fell eight times in a row, so it made one long turn, not repeated swings.

topic_tag: a city library under wartime occupation
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: In a postwar report, one librarian concluded that the occupation had ______ the library.

worlds.passage: For five years of wartime occupation, a city's public library of some three hundred thousand volumes was under the control of the occupying authority. When the staff returned, the open shelves stood full, the forty authors on the authority's banned list among them, and the bound newspapers lay under five years of dust; the room that had held the manuscripts and early printed books was bare. In the 1950s volumes bearing the library's stamp began turning up in the catalogs of three universities in the occupying country. In a postwar report, one librarian concluded that the occupation had ______ the library.
worlds.explanation: The open shelves, banned authors included, stood full while the room of manuscripts and early printed books was bare, and those volumes later surfaced in the occupying country's universities, so the occupation had "plundered" the library. "Purged" fails because the banned authors were left. "Pulped" fails because the volumes survived abroad, and "padlocked" fails because the rare-book room was emptied.

purged.inference: A purge removes the banned authors; they were still on the open shelves, and what went was the room of manuscripts and early printed books, which is a choice by value.

pulped.inference: Pulped books cease to exist; these turned up, still stamped with the library's mark, in the occupying country's universities, so they were carried off, not turned into paper.

padlocked.inference: A library that was only shut keeps its collection; the room of manuscripts and early printed books was empty when the staff returned, so someone had gone in and removed them.

worlds.passage: For five years of wartime occupation, a city's public library of some three hundred thousand volumes was under the control of the occupying authority. pulped.why: The missing books were burned in the square, not sent to a mill to be made into paper.
pulped.surface_fit: Books destroyed under an occupation were often pulped for paper, so the word fits the sentence and the wartime topic.
pulped.inference: Pulping takes bulk paper by weight, and the bulkiest paper, the bound newspapers, was untouched; the missing books matched a banned list and went to a bonfire, destroyed for what they said.

padlocked.quote: About four thousand volumes were missing

padlocked.surface_fit: Occupiers often sealed public buildings for the duration, and padlocked is the ordinary word for a library closed in wartime.
padlocked.inference: A library that was only locked would come back with its shelves complete; four thousand volumes were gone, so someone had worked through the collection.

plundered.inference: A plunderer takes the treasures first; the rare-book room stayed sealed from 1940, and what went was newspapers, textbooks and duplicates by the ton, taken as material, not as prizes.

purged.inference: A purge removes the banned authors; they were left, and what went was whole classes of bulk material measured by weight, which is how one gathers paper stock, not how one censors.

padlocked.surface_fit: Many occupied cities had their libraries closed for the war, so padlocked fits a librarian's account of one.
padlocked.inference: A padlocked library comes back with everything inside; whole floors stood empty, so material was removed in bulk while the building was in the occupiers' hands.

plundered.inference: Plunderers go first to the rare books; a room still sealed with the date 1940 had not been entered since the occupation began, so the library's treasures stayed where they were.

pulped.surface_fit: Wartime paper shortages led many occupiers to pulp books, and bound newspapers are the first thing taken for paper.
pulped.inference: Pulping takes the bulkiest paper first; the bound newspapers lay under dust from 1940 to 1945, so no one removed paper from the library.
